Australia and New Zealand. 11,12 PPS was defined as high-flow nasal prong oxygen (HFNPO) at ³ 1 L/kg/min, nasopharyngeal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP), or mechanical ventilation, and its duration was determined by the unblinded treating clinician. Epinephrine was nebulized using a high gas flow with a large nebulizer fluid volume.
Methods

A pragmatic, open-label, randomized trial was performed at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Starship and Middlemore Hospitals in Auckland, and Perth Children's Hospital. The trial was approved by the Royal Children's Hospital Ethics Committee (Study Number 32119), the Disability Ethics Committee, New Zealand (Study Number NTX/12/05/044/AM04), and the Western Australian Department of Health (Study Number 2020/EP). The trial was registered with the Australian Clinical Trials Research Network (ACTRN12613000316707).
Participants
Children were screened, consented by parents, and randomized at admission to intensive care by members of the study team. Data collection was performed by research assistants and investigators.
Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Children younger than 18 months old with a diagnosis of bronchiolitis were eligible up to 4 hours after admission to intensive care. The diagnosis was based on the presence of a first or second episode of wheezing, or respiratory distress associated with respiratory tract infection, plus either radiologic evidence of chest hyperinflation or clinical evidence of prolonged expiration. Children were excluded if they had received immunosuppressive agents in the previous 7 days, were less than 37 weeks of gestation at enrollment, or had laryngotracheobronchitis, previous enrollment in the study, or treatment with high frequency oscillation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Randomization

Participants were assigned randomly to either the intervention or control group in a 1:1 using an online database to ensure allocation concealment. Randomization was stratified by hospital, the level of PPS at randomization (none, HFNPO-NCPAP, mechanical ventilation), and the presence of either cyanotic congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease requiring oxygen therapy for more than 14 days in the previous 6 months. Block randomization was used with a fixed block size that was not known to the clinicians or investigators. In March 2015, after 50 participants had been recruited, the large number of strata resulted in unequal numbers in the 2 treatment groups. Consequently, the randomization process was modified so the first participant in any new block was randomized with a probability inversely related to the proportion of participants in the 2 groups; for example, if 40% of participants had been randomized to the control group, the new participant would have a 60% chance of being in the control group. After randomization of the first person in a block, subsequent allocations were set to achieve an equal number of intervention and control subjects in that block. Allocation concealment was maintained.
Procedures

Thecontrol group received standard care with no placebo. PPS was administered at the discretion of the treating clinician according to the trial guidelines ( Appendix 1 ; available at www.jpeds.com). Corticosteroids and epinephrine nebulization were permitted in the control group only for postextubation stridor. Selective b -agonist therapy was not permitted. Nasopharyngeal aspirates were recommended but performed at the discretion of the clinician.

In addition to standard care, participants in the intervention group received an initial dose of dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg parenterally) or, if this was not available, an equipotent dose of methylprednisolone (4 mg/kg intravenously) or, if there was no venous access, prednisolone (4 mg/kg enterally); subsequently, prednisolone 1 mg/kg was given enterally every 8 hours for 3 days, then daily for 3 days. With the initial dose of corticosteroid, 5 doses of nebulized epinephrine (0.05 ml/kg of 1% solution or 0.5 ml/kg of 1/1000), made up to 6 mL with 0.9% saline, was administered half hourly, then 1-4 hourly for the first 3 days, then as required for 3 days; nebulization was via MICRO MIST (Hudson RCI) using 12 L/min of oxygen through the ventilation circuit in patients receiving NCPAP or mechanical ventilation, or by mask with HFNPO reduced to 2-4 L/min ( Appendices 1-3 ; available at www.jpeds.com). Study interventions were ceased when the unblinded, treating clinician decided the child was ready for discharge from intensive care.
Outcomes

The primary outcome was the duration of PPS in hours from the time of randomization to discharge from intensive care. In March 2017, the preplanned statistical analysis plan was changed to exclude participants with zero hours of PPS for whom the research question and primary outcome were not relevant (independent of treatment allocation). PPS was managed by the unblinded treating clinicians without a specific weaning protocol until oxygen saturation was 92% or more in low-flow oxygen or room air. Secondary outcomes were time from randomization until the clinician declared readiness for intensive care discharge; the time until actual discharge from intensive care; the time from randomization to hospital discharge; the duration and proportion of participants receiving HFNPO, NCPAP, mechanical ventilation, and NCPAP or mechanical ventilation or both (but not HFNPO); and the number of escalations of respiratory support (from both HFNPO and CPAP). Adverse events including tachycardia, tachyarrhythmias, and hypertension were recorded from randomization until discharge from intensive care. Episodes of hyperglycemia were recorded in the first 72 hours from randomization.

Statistical Analyses

The sample size was based on 1723 children with bronchiolitis admitted to pediatric intensive care units in Australia and New Zealand from 2001 to 2004; the mean of the natural log of the hours of PPS was 4.08 (geometric mean 59.4 hours), with an SD of 1.10. To detect a ratio of 0.60 or less in the duration of PPS (corresponding to a reduction of at least 24 hours of PPS) with 90% power and a P value of .05, 98 patients were needed per group (based on a SD in both groups of 1.10 on the log scale). As only 64% of children received PPS as NCPAP or mechanical ventilation in 2001-2004, the protocol was adjusted to allow for enrolled children who did not receive PPS; therefore, the trial aimed to recruit 153 children per group. However, HFNPO became routine just as the trial started and all but one participant received PPS, so the adjustment was not required; consequently, on November 25th 2019, the Data and Safety Monitoring Committee recommended that the trial cease recruitment because the required number of children receiving PPS (98 in each group) had been recruited. The Trial Management Committee convened on December 9th, 2019 and stopped the study.

An independent Data and Safety Monitoring Committee performed planned interim analyses at 50% and 75% of recruitment using the Haybittle-Peto stopping rule, where early stopping of the trial was recommended only if P < .001 for the primary outcome.

An intention-to-treat analysis was performed with children who did not receive PPS excluded from the primary analysis ( Appendix 4 ; available at www.jpeds.com). Baseline and demographic data were described using frequencies and proportions. The duration of PPS, HFNPO, NCPAP, mechanical ventilation, and intensive care and hospital length of stay were summarized as the geometric mean, plus the mean and SD on the natural log scale. Log-linear regression was used to compare the groups adjusted for the stratification factors used in randomization. Many participants had zero hours of NCPAP plus mechanical ventilation, so for this end point the groups were compared using zero-inflated Poisson regression with robust estimation of variance adjusted for the stratification factors at randomization.

Outcomes regarding the receipt of PPS, HFNPO, NCPAP, and mechanical ventilation from randomization to discharge from intensive care were summarized as the number and proportion of participants requiring each type of support, and the number of escalations of support (HFNPO to NCPAP 1 escalation, NCPAP to mechanical ventilation 1 escalation, and HFNPO to mechanical ventilation 2 escalations). Analysis of escalations was supplemented, post-hoc, with a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Post-hoc analyses were also performed for hours of PPS by sex and age, and for the primary outcome, but including any child who did not receive PPS, with PPS coded as 0.001 hours because the logarithm of zero is undefined. All other analyses were prespecified in the Statistical Analysis Plan.

Sensitivity analyses were performed for the primary outcome, including duration of PPS administered after discharge from intensive care, with adjustment for HPNP, NCPAP, or mechanical ventilation at randomization, and for the primary outcome without adjustment for congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease and post-hoc for the primary outcome including any child who received zero hours of PPS.

Prespecified subgroup analyses of the duration of PPS were performed by the stratification variables and by predefined subgroups: children with congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, prematurity (<37 weeks of gestation), those who tested positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or human metapneumovirus, and respiratory support mode at baseline. Treatment effects between subgroups were compared by including an interaction term in the regression model.
Results

Between July 24, 2013, and November 22, 2019, 211 children were enrolled; 107 were randomized to the intervention group and 104 to the control group. One child in the control group did not receive PPS and was excluded from the analysis but included in a post-hoc sensitivity analysis. Of the 210 remaining participants, 12 were aged <1 month and 14 were aged >12 months. The flow chart of participant recruitment is shown in Figure 1 , and protocol violations in Appendix Table I (available at www.jpeds.com). Baseline characteristics of the participants are shown in Table I . Table II shows the primary and secondary outcomes. Polymerase chain reaction testing of nasopharyngeal aspirates was performed in 197 of the 210 children: RSV was detected in 117 children (59%), human metapneumovirus in 10, and other viruses in 15 ( Appendix Table II ; available at www.jpeds.com). The primary outcome of geometric mean duration of PPS from randomization until discharge from intensive care was 26.4 hours (95% CI 21.8-31.8) in the intervention group and 39.9 hours (95% CI 33.6-47.4) in controls, with an adjusted ratio of 0.66 (95% CI 0.51-0.84), P = .001.

In a sensitivity analysis including extra PPS administered after discharge from intensive care in 6 children, the adjusted ratio of duration of PPS in the intervention compared with the control group was 0.66 (95% CI 0.52-0.85), P = .001 ( Appendix Table III ; available at www.jpeds.com). In a sensitivity analysis including the child in the control group who received no PPS, coded as 0.001 hours of PPS, the adjusted ratio of duration of PPS in the intervention, compared with the control group, was unchanged at 0.66 (0.51-0.84).

For stratification factors and in the preplanned subgroup analysis ( Table III ), there was no evidence that the intervention effect varied by hospital, prematurity (gestation <37 weeks), or infection by human metapneumovirus, but there was evidence of an interaction with chronic lung disease ( P = .025) and infection by RSV ( P = .018). In 117 children with RSV, the adjusted ratio for duration of PPS was 0.49 (95% CI 0.36-0.68) compared with 0.91 (95% CI 0.62-1.35) in those without RSV. Among children on HFNPO or NCPAP at randomization, there were 24 escalations of PPS (from HFNPO to NCPAP, or NCPAP to mechanical ventilation) in the control group (0.23 escalations per child), compared with 14 escalations in the treatment group (0.13 escalations per child), P = .124 ( Figure 2 ; available at www.jpeds.com). Between 9 AM and 6.59 PM, PPS was ceased in 58% of the 210 participants, 84% were discharged from intensive care, and 94% were discharged from hospital ( Appendix Table IV ; available at www.jpeds.com).

In the intervention group, 41 (38%) experienced at least 1 adverse event, compared with 39 (38%) in controls ( Table IV ; available at www.jpeds.com), most commonly sinus tachycardia. One episode of supraventricular tachyarrhythmia occurred in a child receiving nebulized epinephrine via NCPAP which resolved spontaneously. Another child experienced bradycardia and hypotension requiring brief cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but this occurred 48 hours after epinephrine.
Discussion

In children with bronchiolitis requiring intensive care, this pragmatic, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial found strong evidence ( P = .001) that the combination of systemic corticosteroids and nebulized epinephrine reduced the duration of PPS managed by unblinded clinicians. In prospectively planned, secondary analyses, there was strong evidence ( P = .005) that the intervention reduced the time from randomization until a clinician determined that a child was ready for discharge from intensive care, but only weak evidence ( P = .053) of a reduction in the time to actual discharge; there was no evidence of an effect on hospital length of stay; and the intervention almost halved the duration of NCPAP and mechanical ventilation in the sickest children, but they were managed by unblinded clinicians not using a specific weaning protocol. trial would be needed to document a change in intensive care length of stay, and an even larger one to detect a change in hospital length of stay. Adherence to the study protocol was high, with few participants discontinuing therapy.

The intervention halved the duration of PPS in RSVpositive bronchiolitis but had minimal effect in RSVnegative bronchiolitis. Infants with RSV bronchiolitis have metabolome and bacterial metagenome profiles different from those in rhinovirus bronchiolitis, 14 implying that virus-specific effects might influence the response to corticosteroids and epinephrine.

Bronchiolitis is a major cause of hospitalization and admission to intensive care, so these findings have important implications for patients, families, and the cost of health care. 1,2,15 Areduction of 14 hours in the duration of PPS represents a substantial proportion of the 40 hours in the control group. The intervention had only a modest effect on intensive care length of stay ( P = .053) and no effect was observed on hospital length of stay. The 2 main reasons are that the time of discharge is influenced by other factors (such as social considerations) in addition to the need for respiratory support, and that the trial was not powered to detect differences in length of stay. Because 84% of discharges from intensive care and 94% of discharges from hospital occurred during daylight hours (between 9 AM and 6:59 PM), a child who recovered at 8 PM would usually be discharged at the same time as a child who did not recover until 12 hours later at 8 AM the next day, so length of stay in intensive care and in hospital are insensitive to changes in the duration of illness, and a larger trial would be needed to detect an effect on length of stay. There is no widely recognized objective measure of outcome in bronchiolitis 16 ; we chose, as the primary outcome, the duration of PPS as determined by unblinded clinicians. The duration of PPS is measurable and clinically meaningful to children, families, and clinicians.

The PRagmatic Explanatory Continuum Indicator Summary tool for pragmatic or explanatory trials was published after our trial started. 17,18 Wejudged that our trial was mostly 'pragmatic,' with 'explanatory' aspects because we administered the intervention with attention to adherence and recorded the primary outcome in every child.

The only previous randomized trial of corticosteroidepinephrine therapy vs no corticosteroid-sympathomimetic, in emergency departments in Canada, suggested the combination might reduce the need for hospital admission in mild-to-moderate bronchiolitis and is more cost effective than either therapy alone or neither. 19 Our findings suggest an effect in severe disease. Epinephrine may be more effective than albuterol, 20 and there is evidence that the a -adrenergic action of epinephrine may be important in bronchiolitis. 21 These doses were safe, with a similar proportion of treatment and control patients experiencing adverse events, predominantly sinus tachycardia. One brief episode of supraventricular tachycardia during inhaled epinephrine demonstrates the need for monitoring during its administration.

We gave loading and then regular doses of both medications soon after admission to maximize the benefits, and used high nebulizer flows and large volumes to deliver the small droplet sizes needed in infants. 6,7,9,10 In addition to its main role of reducing droplet size, the 0.9% saline used to dilute the epinephrine might have directly affected the outcome, however, any direct effect is likely to have been augmented by epinephrine because, in the Canadian study, epinephrine-saline-corticosteroid was superior to placebo, but saline-corticosteroid was not. 4

The pragmatic design of the trial allowed comparison of corticosteroid-epinephrine with current practice, but it had important limitations. The key limitation was the unblinded design, which might have caused bias because the duration of PPS was determined by unblinded clinicians without a strict weaning protocol (but with unit guidelines that suggest keeping oxygen saturation at 92% or more). A double-blind design would be desirable and would have reduced the risk of bias, but it would not have compared the intervention with current practice, and there was no physiologically inert placebo to nebulize in the control group: in a systematic review of 29 studies, nebulized 0.9% saline improved respiratory signs, suggesting that it may not be a placebo, 3 and nebulized

Only 211 (25%) of 837 eligible children were enrolled because no attempt was made to recruit 383 (46%) children, and consent was obtained from only 211 (51%) of the 411 families approached. The low recruitment rate might have led to selection bias and reduced the generalizability of our findings. To assess its true effect, the intervention needed to be started soon after admission to intensive care, but the requirement that randomization occur within 4 hours challenged both researchers and families. The low consent rate reflected the substantial stress on parents when they are asked to participate in trials in intensive care. 23 Finally, clinicians may have been more likely to escalate therapy or wean slowly in the control arm, especially given that HFNPO was relatively new early in the trial and clinicians may not have yet become comfortable with treating respiratory distress with HFNPO alone.

In children with bronchiolitis in intensive care who required PPS and were managed by unblinded clinicians, compared with standard care, the duration of PPS was reduced by treatment with repeated doses of a combination of systemic corticosteroids and nebulized epinephrine, using a high gas flow and a large volume of fluid in the nebulizer. In prespecified secondary analyses, the effect was strongest in RSV-positive bronchiolitis, and in the sickest children who required NCPAP or mechanical ventilation (managed by unblinded clinicians). The pragmatic design allowed comparison of corticosteroid-epinephrine with current practice, but bias might have occurred because the trial was unblinded, weaning was not protocolized, and because only 25% of eligible children were enrolled. n

abstract: INTRODUCTION: Oxygen therapy through a high-flow nasal cannula is thought to improve the work of breathing and the comfort of patients with acute bronchiolitis. It is widely used in hospital wards and critical care of pediatric patients. However, there is uncertainty on the magnitude of the effect on critical and important outcomes in these patients. OBJECTIVES: The objective of this review is to evaluate the available evidence on the use of oxygen administered through high-flow cannula versus low-flow oxygen for the treatment of acute bronchiolitis in children under two years of age. METHODOLOGY: We carried out a systematic review and a meta-analysis following the PRISMA standards for reporting. The search was carried out in electronic databases by two researchers independently. The evidence was summarized using the GRADE methodology. RESULTS: Six randomized and non-randomized clinical trials were included, including 1867 individuals younger than 24 months of age with acute bronchiolitis in pediatric emergency, hospitalization, and intensive care services. Mortality was not reported in the included studies. Treatment failure occurred in 108/933 in the high flow group and 233/934 in the low flow group (relative risk: 0.46; 95% confidence interval: 0.35 to 0.62), which shows 11.7% less treatment failure (95% confidence interval between 7.9% and 14.5% less) in the high flow group with a number needed to treat of 7.5 (95% confidence interval 6 to 10) with moderate certainty in the evidence. CONCLUSION: The use of humidified and heated oxygen with high flow compared to oxygen at low flow is probably associated with decreased treatment failure in children younger than two years with acute bronchiolitis. There is uncertainty about the effect on hospitalization days and clinical progression.

Palabras clave High flow nasal cannula, Respiration, Artificial, Respiratory Therapy, Oxygen, Oxygen Inhalation Therapy, bronchiolitis, high flow oxygen delivery system
Resumen
Introducción

La terapia con oxígeno a través de cánula nasal de alto flujo actuaría mejorando el trabajo de la respiración y el confort de los pacientes con bronquiolitis aguda. Su uso se encuentra ampliamente difundido en distintas áreas de internación y cuidados críticos de pacientes pediátricos. Sin embargo, existe incertidumbre en la magnitud del efecto en desenlaces críticos e importantes en estos pacientes.
Objetivos

Evaluar la evidencia disponible acerca del uso de oxígeno administrado a través de cánulas de alto flujo, frente a oxígeno a bajo flujo para el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda en menores de dos años.
Metodología

Realizamos una revisión sistemática y metanálisis siguiendo los estándares PRISMA para el reporte de la misma. La búsqueda fue realizada en bases de datos electrónicas por dos investigadores de forma independiente. La evidencia fue resumida utilizando la metodología GRADE.
Resultados

Se incluyeron seis ensayos clínicos aleatorizados y no aleatorizados, incluyendo 1867 individuos menores de 24 meses de edad con bronquiolitis aguda en servicios de emergencias, internación y cuidados intensivos pediátricos. La mortalidad no fue reportada en los estudios incluidos. El fracaso del tratamiento ocurrió en 108/933 en el grupo alto flujo y 233/934 en el grupo bajo flujo (riesgo relativo: 0,46; intervalo de confianza 95%: 0,35 a 0,62), lo que muestra 11,7% menos fracaso de tratamiento (intervalo de confianza 95%: entre 7,9% y 14,5% menos) en el grupo alto flujo con un número necesario a tratar de 7,5 (de 6 a 10) con moderada certeza en la evidencia.
[DOCLING_PAGE 2]
Conclusión

La utilización de oxígeno humidificado y calentado con alto flujo en comparación con el oxígeno a bajo flujo probablemente se asocie con una disminución del fracaso de tratamiento en niños menores de dos años con bronquiolitis aguda. Existe incertidumbre en el efecto sobre los días de internación y puntajes clínicos de progresión.
Abstract
Introduction

Oxygen therapy through a high-flow nasal cannula is thought to improve the work of breathing and the comfort of patients with acute bronchiolitis. It is widely used in hospital wards and critical care of pediatric patients. However, there is uncertainty on the magnitude of the effect on critical and important outcomes in these patients.
Objectives

The objective of this review is to evaluate the available evidence on the use of oxygen administered through high-flow cannula versus low-flow oxygen for the treatment of acute bronchiolitis in children under two years of age.
Methodology

We carried out a systematic review and a meta-analysis following the PRISMA standards for reporting. The search was carried out in electronic databases by two researchers independently. The evidence was summarized using the GRADE methodology.
Results

Six randomized and non-randomized clinical trials were included, including 1867 individuals younger than 24 months of age with acute bronchiolitis in pediatric emergency, hospitalization, and intensive care services. Mortality was not reported in the included studies. Treatment failure occurred in 108/933 in the high flow group and 233/934 in the low flow group (relative risk: 0.46; 95% confidence interval: 0.35 to 0.62), which shows 11.7% less treatment failure (95% confidence interval between 7.9% and 14.5% less) in the high flow group with a number needed to treat of 7.5 (95% confidence interval 6 to 10) with moderate certainty in the evidence.
Conclusion

The use of humidified and heated oxygen with high flow compared to oxygen at low flow is probably associated with decreased treatment failure in children younger than two years with acute bronchiolitis. There is uncertainty about the effect on hospitalization days and clinical progression.
Ideas clave
La bronquiolitis es la infección más frecuente del tracto respiratorio inferior en los lactantes y representa una causa importante de hospitalización en este grupo de edad.
La terapia con oxígeno a través de cánula nasal de alto flujo se encuentra ampliamente difundida en el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda del lactante.
Existe incertidumbre en el efecto sobre desenlaces críticos en estos pacientes.
Realizamos una revisión sistemática de alta calidad metodológica y valoramos el cuerpo de la evidencia utilizando metodología GRADE.
Esta intervención probablemente se asocie con una disminución del fracaso de tratamiento.
La evidencia acumulada hasta el momento es insuficiente para valorar su impacto en la mortalidad.
[DOCLING_PAGE 3]
Introducción

La bronquiolitis es la infección más frecuente del tracto respiratorio inferior en los lactantes y representa una causa importante de hospitalización en este grupo de edad. Se estima que entre 11 y 12% de los lactantes se ven afectados en el primer año de vida, y entre 1 y 2% de ellos requieren hospitalización 1 . De los admitidos en salas de emergencia e internación, el 10% de los niños previamente sanos y 36% de aquellos con comorbilidades, requerirán internación en una unidad de cuidados intensivos pediátricos. Este grupo de niños presenta una mortalidad asociada del 1% 2,3 .

El tratamiento mediante la tradicional administración de oxigenoterapia a bajo flujo con máscara o cánula nasal presenta limitaciones derivadas de la aplicación de oxígeno seco y la imposibilidad de utilizar alto flujo 4,5 .

Cuando este enfoque terapéutico es ineficaz, se utilizan las estrategias de ventilación no invasiva, principalmente a través de la aplicación de la presión positiva continua en las vías respiratorias.

La aplicación de ventilación no invasiva presenta dificultades en los lactantes pequeños, especialmente en aquellos con peso inferior a siete kilogramos. Además de las limitantes técnicas relacionadas con la interface utilizada, los flujos generados y el equipamiento disponible, la aplicación de presión positiva continua en las vías respiratorias/ventilación no invasiva puede ser un desafío, requiere personal de enfermería y médico altamente capacitado, no siempre es tolerado por los pacientes y, por lo tanto, en el pasado se ha restringido a la unidad de cuidados intensivos 6,7 .

La terapia de oxígeno con cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada calentada, proporciona gas calentado y humidificado con alto flujo con el objetivo de mejorar el trabajo respiratorio y el confort de los pacientes. El añadir calor y altos niveles de humidificación, permite emplear flujos elevados de aire y oxígeno, logrando concentraciones cercanas al 100%. Para ello se requiere de sistemas con mezcladores de oxígeno y flujímetros adecuados. Estos sistemas de oxigenación de alto flujo son cómodos, sencillos y tienen la ventaja de no interferir con la alimentación 8,9 .

En las salas de pediatría, la oxigenoterapia de alto flujo a través de una cánula nasal, se ha convertido en un nuevo método ampliamente difundido para proporcionar apoyo respiratorio para enfermedades respiratorias en lactantes y recién nacidos. Existen estudios clínicos en infantes con bronquiolitis aguda que muestran beneficios en algunos desenlaces subrogados (frecuencia respiratoria, días de internación, entre otros) 10 .

Nos propusimos realizar una revisión sistemática para sintetizar la evidencia disponible acerca del uso de oxígeno a través de cánula nasal de alto flujo comparada con oxígeno a bajo flujo para el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda de los niños menores de dos años.
Métodos

Se conformó un equipo multidisciplinario libre de conflictos de interés, para realizar una revisión sistemática acerca del uso de cánulas de alto flujo frente al oxígeno administrado, a través de sistemas de bajo flujo para el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda en la población de niños menores de dos años.
Este estudio se realizó siguiendo los lineamientos PRISMA ( Prefered Reported Items in Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis ) para la realización y publicación de revisiones sistemáticas 11 .
El protocolo fue publicado previamente en registro PROSPERO de revisiones sistemáticas ( PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Review ). Número de registro: CRD42020169993 12 .
Pregunta de investigación
¿Debería usarse cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada calentada frente a la terapia convencional con oxígeno a bajo flujo para el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda en niños menores de 2 años?
Pregunta PICO
P: pacientes menores de 24 meses con diagnóstico presuntivo de bronquiolitis aguda.
I: cánula nasal con oxígeno a alto flujo.
C: oxígeno a bajo flujo.

O: mortalidad, fracaso del tratamiento (definido como necesidad de ventilación no invasiva o intubación), puntaje de severidad, duración de la internación, eventos adversos relacionados con el tratamiento.
Fuentes de datos

Dos revisores en forma independiente realizaron una búsqueda sensible, en las siguientes bases de datos bibliográficas: PubMed, EMBASE, LILACS, Cochrane Library, Epistemonikos y Tripdatabase. Asimismo, se realizó una búsqueda de otras fuentes y repositorios de agencias de evaluación de tecnologías sanitarias y agencias nacionales e internacionales. Se realizó una matriz de evidencia a fin de identificar entre los estudios primarios que integraban las distintas revisiones sistemáticas seleccionadas inicialmente, trabajos que no hubieran surgido de otras estrategias de búsqueda. También se realizaron búsquedas adicionales de las referencias a través de Cross-Ref.
Este es el ejemplo de estrategia de búsqueda en Medline/PubMed, que incluyó los siguientes términos:

No se realizó restricción por idioma. Además, con el fin de identificar literatura adicional, se buscaron en el motor de búsqueda Google Scholar y se contactó a expertos. Estas búsquedas se realizaron de acuerdo con el tipo de plataforma y se usaron en la búsqueda términos de lenguaje libre. Las búsquedas fueron llevadas a cabo hasta el 1 de julio de 2020.
En el Anexo 1, podrán obtenerse más detalles acerca de la búsqueda completa.
Selección de estudios

Se buscaron ensayos aleatorios controlados, estudios no aleatorios, prospectivos y analíticos que incluyan una rama control en niños menores de 24 meses de edad con diagnóstico presuntivo de bronquiolitis aguda, donde la intervención fuera cánula nasal con oxígeno a alto flujo, y el comparador alguna forma de administración de oxígeno a bajo flujo.
[DOCLING_PAGE 4]

Se tomaron en cuenta los siguientes desenlaces en orden de relevancia clínica: muerte (crítico, 9), fracaso del tratamiento, definido como necesidad de asistencia ventilatoria mecánica o de ventilación no invasiva (asistencia ventilatoria mecánica o ventilación no invasiva) (crítico, 7), días de internación (importante, 6), puntajes de severidad (importante, 4), eventos adversos (no importante, 3).
Recolección de datos

Los estudios fueron seleccionados por dos revisores en forma independiente basados en los criterios de inclusión y exclusión. Las diferencias se definieron por acuerdo entre los mismos. Se revisaron, además, las referencias de las revisiones sistemáticas identificadas. Dos revisores extractaron en forma independiente la evidencia de los desenlaces seleccionados en planillas en formato electrónico diseñadas para tal fin.
Riesgo de sesgo

Se realizó la valoración del riesgo de sesgo a través de la herramienta de riesgo de sesgos sugerida por Cochrane (RoB-2) 13 . Dos operadores evaluaron independientemente el riesgo de sesgo de los ensayos (Anexo 2 y Figura 2). Para cada ensayo y desenlace, los revisores los calificaron en:
Bajo riesgo de sesgo.
ii) Algunas inquietudes, probablemente bajo riesgo de sesgo.
iii) Algunas inquietudes, probablemente alto riesgo de sesgo.
iv) Alto riesgo de sesgo.

Dominios del riesgo de sesgo: sesgo que surge del proceso de asignación al azar; sesgo debido a desviaciones de la intervención prevista; sesgo debido los datos de resultado faltantes; sesgo en la medición del resultado; sesgo en la selección de los informes de resultados, incluidas las desviaciones del protocolo registrado; y sesgo que surge de la terminación anticipada en beneficio.
Las diferencias entre los operadores fueron definidas por un tercero en el caso que resultase necesario.
Medidas de efecto y análisis estadístico

Se realizó el análisis de los resultados utilizando riesgo relativo para desenlaces binarios y diferencia de medias para desenlaces continuos, junto con su intervalo de confianza 95%. Para el metanálisis se utilizó el modelo de efectos aleatorios de Mantel y Haenszel.

Para los cálculos meta-analíticos, riesgo de sesgo, sesgo de publicación y realización de gráficos de tipo semáforo, sumario, forest plot y funnel plot , se utilizó R ( RStudio Version 1.3.1073 © 2009-2020 RStudio, PBC ).
Certeza en la evidencia

El enfoque GRADE ( Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation ) se utilizó para evaluar la certeza en el cuerpo de evidencia para cada comparación. Para la realización de las tablas de resumen de hallazgos se utilizó la herramienta GRADE, y se extrajo en planillas la información acerca de los estudios y desenlaces incluidos. Posteriormente, se realizó la síntesis de los estudios seleccionados y se realizó la construcción de los perfiles de evidencia con ayuda del portal 14,15 .

Calificamos la certeza para cada comparación y desenlace como alta, moderada, baja o muy baja, basándonos en los campos de evaluación de riesgo de sesgo, inconsistencia, evidencia indirecta, sesgo de publicación e imprecisión.
Los perfiles de evidencia GRADE están disponibles en la Tabla 2 y en el Anexo 2.
Análisis del poder de la muestra y tamaño óptimo de intervención

Para detectar el apropiado poder de la muestra se realizó el cálculo del tamaño óptimo de intervención, utilizando R ( RStudio Version 1.3.1073 © 2009-2020 RStudio, PBC ), asumiendo un efecto d (el tamaño del efecto general hipotético o plausible de una intervención en el estudio en comparación con el control) de SMD 0,15, un número k de estudios de 5, el número de pacientes en ramas intervención y control de 200 (n1 y n2) y un nivel α de 0,05 y moderada heterogeneidad, con un poder de 81,75%.
Análisis de subgrupo y sesgo de publicación

Se plantearon análisis de subgrupo de acuerdo con el riesgo de sesgo de los estudios incluidos (bajo versus alto riesgo de sesgo: RoB_BAJO versus RoB_ALTO). Se analizó la presencia de sesgo de publicación a través de la realización de un gráfico de tipo funnel plot y a través del estadístico de la prueba de Eggers 16 .
Resultados
Luego de la selección, seis de los estudios fueron incluidos en la síntesis cuantitativa y sus resultados meta-analizados (Figura 1).

Los participantes fueron en todos los casos menores de 24 meses, mientras que en dos estudios sólo incluyeron menores de 12 meses y en otro exclusivamente, menores de seis meses. El escenario clínico fue en todos los casos el ámbito de la internación, área de emergencias y cuidados críticos pediátricos. La intervención utilizada fue cánula nasal con oxígeno humidificado y calentado en alto flujo con un flujo de 1 a 2 litros por kilogramo por minuto, con un máximo en todos los casos de 20 litros. El comparador fue oxígeno a bajo flujo con cánula nasal o con máscara con oxígeno al 100%. Encontramos un resumen de los estudios incluidos en esta revisión 17-22 en la Tabla 1.

Desenlace muerte

La mayoría de los estudios incluidos en esta revisión no reportaron el desenlace muerte. Uno de ellos, Kepreotes y colaboradores 2017 17 , reportó que no existieron muertes durante el período de seguimiento.
Desenlace fracaso del tratamiento

Presentaron fracaso del tratamiento (necesidad de ventilación no invasiva, invasiva o intubación oro traqueal) 108/933 en el grupo de cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada y 233/934 en el grupo bajo flujo (riesgo relativo: 0,46; intervalo de confianza: 95% 0,35 a 0,62). Esto significa en números absolutos 11,7% menos fracaso de tratamiento (intervalo de confianza: 95% entre 7,9% y 14,5% menos) en el grupo de cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada (Tabla 2).
La certeza en la evidencia respecto a este desenlace fue moderada debido al alto riesgo de sesgo en los estudios incluidos (Figura 3 forest plot ).

Desenlace días de internación

Los pacientes tratados con cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada respecto a los tratados con bajo flujo tuvieron una diferencia de media en los días de internación de -0,55 (entre 1,92 días menos y 0,85 días más) (Figura 4).

La certeza en la evidencia en este desenlace fue muy baja debido a imprecisión (amplios intervalos de confianza que incluyen riesgos y beneficios), heterogeneidad (I2 elevado, superposición de los intervalos de confianza) y riesgo de sesgo de los estudios incluidos.

Desenlace puntajes de severidad

Los puntajes de severidad utilizados variaron ampliamente entre los estudios. Mientras que Hilliard y colaboradores 18 no reportaron cambios en los puntajes de severidad, Franklin y colaboradores 19 , Ergul y colaboradores 21 , y Milani y colaboradores 22 utilizaron parámetros clínicos como la frecuencia y el esfuerzo respiratorio y la capacidad para alimentarse, que fueron reportados luego como desenlaces individuales en respuesta al tratamiento.

Kepreotes y colaboradores 17 por su parte, valoraron inicialmente a los niños a través del puntaje Health Initial Severity Assessment of Bronchiolitis , que incluye también diferentes parámetros clínicos como la cianosis y la saturación de oxígeno, utilizando estos parámetros para valorar fracaso del tratamiento y tiempo hasta el fracaso del tratamiento.

Por último, Bueno Campaña y colaboradores 20 utilizaron el Respiratory Distress Assessment Instrument (o RDAI por sus siglas en inglés) en el cual se mide la presencia de sibilancias, crepitantes y retracción costal. Para medir la eficacia del tratamiento asignado se utilizó el cambio en este puntaje antes y después del tratamiento. En este estudio, no se encontraron diferencias entre las medias de ambos grupos (p = 0,24): diferencia de medias -1,22 (int ervalo de confianza 95%: 2,99 a 0,55).

Los estudios incluidos no reportaron eventos adversos relacionados con la intervención o el comparador.

Discusión
Las estimaciones absolutas y relativas de efecto y la importancia de los desenlaces pueden observarse con detalle en la Tabla 2 de resumen de hallazgos.
[DOCLING_PAGE 9]

Este metanálisis fue realizado con altos estándares de calidad, siguiendo normativas destinadas a la realización y presentación de revisiones sistemáticas, junto a metanálisis PRISMA. Incluimos la mejor evidencia disponible a través de una exhaustiva revisión de la literatura y valoración del riesgo de sesgo dentro de los estudios incluidos y el sesgo de publicación entre los estudios. Asimismo, el resumen de la evidencia se realizó utilizando la metodología GRADE para determinar las estimaciones de efecto y el grado de certeza del cuerpo de la literatura incluida en la revisión.

La evidencia analizada, muestra que el uso de oxígeno a través de cánula de alto flujo humidificado y calentado, probablemente se asocie con una reducción absoluta del 11,7% en el fracaso del tratamiento en infantes con bronquiolitis aguda en menores de 24 meses, debiendo tratar 7,5 pacientes con la intervención para reducir un evento (número necesario a tratar 7,5; intervalo de confianza 95%: de 6 a 10).

En cuanto a los días de internación, existe incertidumbre en la magnitud del efecto de la cánula nasal de alto flujo humidificada respecto al tratamiento estándar, por lo que la terapia con oxígeno de alto flujo podría no estar asociada con cambio en los días de internación. Esto se encuentra sustentado en una baja certeza de la evidencia debido a la imprecisión y riesgo de sesgo de los estudios incluidos.

No pudimos evaluar apropiadamente la mortalidad dado que, en los estudios que se revisaron la misma se mantuvo por debajo del 1%. En las cohortes de seguimiento de pacientes con bronquiolitis aguda, la mortalidad no fue reportada, por lo tanto, no existe evidencia disponible del efecto del oxígeno de alto flujo sobre la muerte en el tratamiento de la bronquiolitis aguda en este grupo etario.

Por otro lado, los puntajes de severidad no fueron incluidos debido a que no pudieron ser valorados apropiadamente, dado que existe una gran imprecisión en el momento de utilización de estos, en los tipos de puntajes evaluados y en el reporte apropiado de los mismos.
No se reportaron eventos adversos relacionados con la intervención o el control.
Conclusiones

La utilización de oxígeno humidificado y calentado con alto flujo en comparación con el oxígeno a bajo flujo, probablemente se asocia con una disminución del fracaso de tratamiento en niños menores de dos años con bronquiolitis aguda.
Existe incertidumbre en la magnitud del efecto en los días de internación y en los puntajes clínicos de progresión.
La evidencia disponible es insuficiente para valorar el efecto de la intervención en la mortalidad en la población evaluada.

We conducted a trial of 50 children with bronchiolitis who were randomized to treatment with CPAP or HFNC. Objectives were to compare the development in respiratory rate, pCO2, and Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) in young children with bronchiolitis, treated with CPAP or HFNC. Secondarily, to compare Neonatal Infant Pain Score (NIPS), treatment duration, treatment failure, and hospitalization length. Median age at inclusion was 2.8 (CPAP group) vs 2.1 months (HFNC group). Mean baseline pCO2 was 6.7 in both groups and mean respiratory rate was 60 vs 56 in the CPAP and HFNC group respectively. No differences were observed in development of respiratory rate, pCO2, or M-WCAS. NIPS was higher in the CPAP group. Treatment failure was scarce in both groups. No significant differences in treatment duration or length of hospitalization were observed.Conclusion: In infants and young children with bronchiolitis, HFNC may be an effective and pleasant alternative to CPAP. Abstract

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) has been used in infants with bronchiolitis for decades. Recently, high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy was introduced. We conducted a trial of 50 children with bronchiolitis who were randomized to treatment with CPAP or HFNC. Objectives were to compare the development in respiratory rate, pCO2, and Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) in young children with bronchiolitis, treated with CPAP or HFNC. Secondarily, to compare Neonatal Infant Pain Score (NIPS), treatment duration, treatment failure, and hospitalization length. Median age at inclusion was 2.8 (CPAP group) vs 2.1 months (HFNC group). Mean baseline pCO2 was 6.7 in both groups and mean respiratory rate was 60 vs 56 in the CPAP and HFNC group respectively. No differences were observed in development of respiratory rate, pCO2, or MWCAS.NIPSwashigher in the CPAP group. Treatment failure was scarce in both groups. No significant differences in treatment duration or length of hospitalization were observed.

Conclusion : In infants and young children with bronchiolitis, HFNC may be an effective and pleasant alternative to CPAP. Larger multicenter studies are needed to further explore differences in treatment failure and treatment duration.
Trial registration : www.clinicaltrial.gov. id NCT02618213, registration date December 1, 2015.
What is Known:

CPAPhas been used for many years for respiratory support in infant bronchiolitis. The method requires special staff skills and may be stressful to the child. · HFNC has been introduced as a newer tool.
What is New:
In infants with bronchiolitis, HFNC and CP AP were comparable in decreasing respiratory rate, pCO2, and need for oxygen supply.
Pain score during therapy was lower in the HFNC group.

Introduction

Viral bronchiolitis is often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and is a major cause of disease burden in infants and young children. RSV infections present with symptoms from mild coryza to fulminant respiratory failure and are a major cause of hospitalization in young children. Thus, in Denmark, approximately 3% of children under 2 years of age experience at least one hospitalization due to RSV [4]. Because of airway obstruction, alveolar atelectasis, decreased oxygenation, and increased respiratory work, some children progress to severe respiratory distress and need for noninvasive respiratory support or mechanical ventilation.

In Denmark, the standard treatment for infants and young children with respiratory distress due to moderate to severe bronchiolitis has for many years been continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Although not fully understood, CPAP may work by small airway distension, mucus wash out, and delivery of high flow oxygen [13]. CPAP has been shown to lower respiratory rate and pCO2 better than standard care [14] and has been associated with decreased intubation rates [3]. However, the therapy requires special staff skills, close monitoring, and can be stressful to the child.

Recently, high flow oxygenation therapy (HFNC) was introduced as an alternative tool in the management of respiratory distress due to bronchiolitis. HFNC delivers a heated, humidified gas with a mixture of oxygen and air, washes out dead space, and has some CPAP effect [11]. In a few bronchiolitis studies, HFNC proved to be better than standard care [1] [7]. Furthermore HFNC has been shown to give a better patient tolerance, less nose damage, and less work for the staff than CPAP [12].

We conducted a two-center prospective open randomized trial of HFNC and CPAP to explore effects of treatment with these two systems on respiratory variables in infants and young children with bronchiolitis.
Materials and methods
Patients

Bronchiolitis was defined as an acute respiratory illness in children < 2 years of age presenting with characteristic patterns of wheeze and cough. Criteria for respiratory support were based on clinical and paraclinical signs of respiratory failure: High respiratory rate (RR), retractions, recurrent apnea, hypercapnia, and acidosis.

Inclusion criteria for this study were children with bronchiolitis and need for respiratory support as assessed by the pediatrician in charge. Furthermore, informed consent from all parents/legal guardians should be obtained before randomization.
Exclusion criteria were previous chronic disease or severe respiratory insufficiency with decreased consciousness, need for urgent treatment, and/or a capillary pCO2 > 9.0.

The patient registration system was searched to evaluate the frequency of children with an ICD10 diagnose code of DJ960*, DJ21*, DJ205*, or DJ12* and the procedure code BGFC32 during the study period included.
Settings

The study was conducted between December 2015 and May 2018. During the first two seasons, the study took place at the pediatric department at the Hospital of South West Jutland, Denmark, and during the last seasons also at the department of pediatrics at Kolding Hospital, Denmark.

All children fulfilling the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria were invited to participate. Because of the nature of this study, blinding was not possible. Randomization was conducted in blocks of four, stratified per center, and treatment allocation envelopes were stored in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes, prefabricated by a person outside the study. By mistake, the first 20 patients were however randomized by simple lot, conducted by a person outside the study.
For CPAP, a binasal prong with a Benveniste valve connected to a humidifier (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare® Auckland, New Zealand) was used. The initial flow was 12 -14 L/min.
For HFNC, we used Optiflow Junior (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare® Auckland, New Zealand). Three sizes of nasal prongs were used, according to the weight of the child. The initial flow was 2 l/kg/min.
In both systems, flow could be increased to a maximum of 15/l/min and oxygen supply was delivered as needed to maintain a SpO2 above 92%.
Observations and paraclinical examination

PCR analysis of nasopharyngeal mucus for RSV was routinely analyzed in all patients. Chest x-ray was conducted prior to treatment and described by a radiologist. Capillary gas values (pH, pCO2) were conducted prior to treatment and after 6, 12, 24, and 48 h of treatment.

All children were intensively observed by a trained nurse. For this study, heart rate (HR), RR, and oxygen supply were registered at treatment start and every 6 h for the first 24 h and then once daily.
[DOCLING_PAGE 3]

Modified Woods Clinical Asthma Score (M-WCAS) [15] is a combined score (0 -10) used to evaluate the degree of respiratory distress in children with bronchiolitis. M-WCAS has been validated for use in hospitalized children with bronchiolitis and includes evaluation of oxygen saturation, inspiratory breath sounds, expiratory wheezing, use of accessory respiratory muscles, and cerebral function [2].
The physician in charge assessed all the included children with the M-WCAS before initiation of treatment and then once daily.

Neonatal Infant Pain Score [5] (NIPS) was used in the last season of inclusion in children younger than 2 months. The score is a validated system based on facial mimic, cry, breathing habitant, arm and leg tonus, and consciousness. A total of 0 -8 points can be achieved, where 0 represents no pain, and eight maximal pain. The children were scored shortly after initiation of therapy and then once daily. For children older than 2 months, the 0 -10 point Face Leg Activity Cry and Consolability (FLACC) score [6] was used.
For this study, scores were also given as percent of maximum score in order to merge data in a combined pain score regardless of age.
Treatment length was recorded as net time, excluding breaks. Breaks mainly occurred when the condition of the child improved, as an attempt to discontinue treatment.

Treatment failure was assessed by the physician in charge who also decided whether it should lead to a switch of system (CPAP to HFNC/HFNC to CPAP) or to transmission to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) with or without initiation of mechanical ventilation prior to transportation.

Retrospectively, we searched the electronic patient database for infants and young children hospitalized with RSVrelated disease (DJ121, DJ205, DJ210) during the study period. The purpose of this was to estimate the fraction of CPAP/ HFNC support, and the fraction of study participants in this population.
Outcomes
Primary outcomes were change in pCO2, RR, and M-WCAS from time 0 to 48 h after initiation of the treatment. Change in fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) was added as an unplanned analysis.
Secondary outcomes were differences in pain scores, treatment duration, and frequency of system failure.
Statistical analysis

Sample size calculation was conducted based on the primary outcome pCO2. Assuming a difference of one kPa at 48 h and considering an α error of 5% and a β error at 20%, a sample size of 48 participants was calculated.
For group comparisons, two-sided Student ' s t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for normally and nonnormally distributed data respectively. Chi 2 test was used for binary outcomes.

Developments in RR, pCO2, M-WCAS, FiO2, and pain scores (NIPS, FLACC, and combined pain score) were measured using a random intercept model with maximum likelihood estimation. Device, time, and interaction between these were chosen as explanatory variables. Post estimation analysis was conducted using residual diagnostics. For the primary outcomes, the model was then extended with season and site, to explore effects of these.
Comparisons of treatment duration and length of hospitalization were conducted using log rank test for equality.
For all analyses, significance level was defined as p < 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using STATA10 statistical software.
Ethics

The study was prospectively approved by the Regional Committee on Health Research Ethics for Southern Denmark, the Danish Data Protection Agency, and registered as a clinical trial at Clinicaltrials.gov. A protocol amendment was approved prior to the third season, regarding extension with another center and the use of pain scores. Written informed consent was collected from all legal guardians before any study-related procedures took place. In cases of only one present guardian, a prospectively written authorization from the absent guardian to the present guardian, regarding decision about participation, was accepted.
Results

During the study period, a total of 266 children were hospitalized with RSV-related disease. Of these, 99 children were treated with CPAP/HFNC for viral bronchiolitis at the two sites and 50 children were included in the study (22 HFNC/ 28 CPAP). During the first 48 h, ten children left the study. Eight children (5 CPAP/3 HFNC) left due to cessation of need for respiratory support and two children (both CPAP) left because of disease progression leading to transmission to the PICU. Four of the ten children were withdrawn during the first 24 h, including the two children in need of intensive care and one from each group due to cessation of need for respiratory support.
Table 1 describes the 50 children included. No differences were seen between the groups in baseline demographic or respiratory variables.

RR, pCO2, FiO2 (Fig. 1), and M-WCAS (Table 2) all declined during the first 48 h of treatment. No differences between the groups were seen. FiO2 showed a tendency towards faster decline in the CPAP group; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.07).

Including season and site in the model had no effect on pCO2, M-CWAS, or FiO2. There was effect of site on the development in RR (coefficient 7.3, p > 0.05) with the children from Kolding having a lower RR. However, this did not affect the development in RR in the model.

During the first treatment day, NIPS was lower in the HFNCgroup right after initiation of therapy but declined with time in both groups (Table 2). There was however an overall effect of system in the regression model (coefficient -0.94. p < 0.05) meaning that NIPS was overall lower in the HFNC group. FLACC score was not analyzed, due to the few children assessed with this score. The combined pain score showed similar results as NIPS (Table 2).

The CPAP group had a median treatment time of 70 (6 -240) hours and the HFNC group of 95 (27 -193) hours. However, this difference of 25 h did not reach statistical significance. A similar and non-significant difference was seen in length of hospitalization.

There were few treatment failures in both groups. Four children (two from each group) were switched to the opposite system because of disease progression (HFNC) or poor system tolerance (CPAP). In addition, two CPAP children were transferred to the PICU because of treatment failure. Between groups, there were no statistical differences in frequency of treatment failure or in PICU transferal.
Discussion

In this study, no differences were found in the primary outcomes, suggesting that HFNC may be a good alternative to CPAP in children with bronchiolitis. Our study suggests a better patient acceptance of HFNC compared with CPAP as measured by the NIPS and the combined pain score, which corroborate earlier findings [9, 12]. Sarkar et al. [12] also found less nose damage with HFNC, an outcome not investigated in the present study.
Fig. 1 Development in mean respiratory rate, FiO2, or pCO2 during 48 h of respiratory support. No significant differences were observed between the groups

To our knowledge, only few studies compared CPAP and HFNC in management of bronchiolitis. In a retrospective study, Pedersen et al. found that CPAP was superior to HFNC in lowering RR and FiO2 [10]. A multicenter study including 142 children found a higher success rate in the group treated with CPAP [9]. However, two other small studies [8, 12] found the two systems equally effective in lowering of RR, PCO2, etc.
The differences between our study and earlier findings may be explained by differences in patient populations. From the

present literature, there might be an indication of superiority of CPAP over HFNC, when treating severely ill children with bronchiolitis [9, 10]. In the present study, and in the study by Sarkar et al. [12], an upper pCO 2 limit may have excluded more severely ill children, whereas Milesi et al. [9] only excluded children with urgent need for intubation or radiologistverified atelectasis. This may account for some of the differences in results and could indicate that HFNC mainly is an alternative tool in less severe bronchiolitis.

In Denmark, there is a strong tradition for CPAP, and it is likely that it is used in less sick children than elsewhere, which could hamper the comparison between studies. However, CPAP/HFNC was not used more frequently in the years of this study, compared with the two previous seasons [10]. Whether some of the less sick children would have benefited equally to conservative treatment (oxygen, feeding supply, etc.) is a question that goes beyond the purpose for this study.

The use of the change in pCO2, a highly variable parameter of modest clinical relevance, for sample size calculation could be considered as a weakness in the study design. However, we see no signs of clinically relevant differences in our primary outcomes (Fig. 1). Moreover, the size of our study population is comparable with or bigger than for other studies [8, 12].

Only half of the children admitted with viral bronchiolitis and treated with CPAP/HFNC were included in the study. The major cause was failure to obtain informed consent from both parents because only one of the parents/legal guardians was present at the hospital. Others declined participation or meet an exclusion criterion.

The 48-h observation period in our study was chosen to minimize treatment termination within the period, as it was expected that most children would need at least 48 h of treatment. Moreover, we expected that the main effects would occur during this time span. The termination of treatment before 48 h in ten children may have affected the results. However, the dropouts were relatively equally distributed between the two groups, and furthermore, it was only children from the CPAP group who left due to a deterioration of the condition resulting in intensive care. Overall, we do not consider that dropouts during the first 48 h affected the results in favor of HFNC.

Despite a clinically relevant difference of 25 h, no statistically significant difference in treatment length between the groups was found. We suppose that this is primarily due to the lack of power in our study. However, the transferal of two children from the CPAP group to PICU (who therefore were withdrawn from the analysis) may have contributed to the difference in average treatment length. In the present study, treatment failures were few and equally distributed in the two groups. This is in contrast to earlier findings. In a retrospective study, Pedersen et al. [14] found a higher failure rate within the HFNC group, and in a multicenter study including 142 children, Milesi et al. found a higher success rate in the group treated with CPAP [9].

As our study was not powered to show non-inferiority, our results should be followed up, preferably by larger multicenter studies with statistical power to explore this. Also, clinically relevant outcomes like treatment duration, treatment failure, and intubation rates could not be investigated sufficiently in the present study. Hereby, possible differences in patient acceptance, side effects, and staff resource costs within the different treatment systems could be the aim for further investigation.

In conclusion, we found HFNC to be a safe and effective tool for respiratory support in young children with moderatesevere bronchiolitis. We found similar effects on RR, MWCAS, and pC02 compared with CPAP. Pain scores were significantly lower in the HFNC group indicating better patient acceptance. More research is warranted to further explore target groups for each of the two systems.

title: High flow nasal cannula and continuous positive airway pressure therapy in treatment of viral bronchiolitis: a randomized clinical trial.

abstract: PURPOSE: Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) is currently the gold standard for respiratory support for moderate to severe acute viral bronchiolitis (AVB). Although oxygen delivery via high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is increasingly used, evidence of its efficacy and safety is lacking in infants. METHODS: A randomized controlled trial was performed in five pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) to compare 7 cmH(2)O nCPAP with 2 L/kg/min oxygen therapy administered with HFNC in infants up to 6 months old with moderate to severe AVB. The primary endpoint was the percentage of failure within 24 h of randomization using prespecified criteria. To satisfy noninferiority, the failure rate of HFNC had to lie within 15% of the failure rate of nCPAP. Secondary outcomes included success rate after crossover, intubation rate, length of stay, and serious adverse events. RESULTS: From November 2014 to March 2015, 142 infants were included and equally distributed into groups. The risk difference of -19% (95% CI -35 to -3%) did not allow the conclusion of HFNC noninferiority (p = 0.707). Superiority analysis suggested a relative risk of success 1.63 (95% CI 1.02-2.63) higher with nCPAP. The success rate with the alternative respiratory support, intubation rate, durations of noninvasive and invasive ventilation, skin lesions, and length of PICU stay were comparable between groups. No patient had air leak syndrome or died. CONCLUSION: In young infants with moderate to severe AVB, initial management with HFNC did not have a failure rate similar to that of nCPAP. This clinical trial was recorded in the National Library of Medicine registry (NCT 02457013).

Keywords: Bronchiolitis, Continuous positive airway pressure, High flow nasal cannula, Infant, Noninvasive ventilation, Oxygen inhalation therapy, Randomized controlled trial, Respiratory syncytial virus infections, Respiratory therapy
Introduction

Acute viral bronchiolitis (AVB) is the most common respiratory infection in infancy and the leading cause of hospitalization among infants in high-income countries [1]. While most cases require supportive management only, a severe form of illness observed in 8-13% of the cases requires hospitalization in a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for evolving respiratory distress [2]. Although AVB may present as a restrictive parenchymal disease, most of these infants have severe obstructive lung disease [3] with markedly increased inspiratory load [4, 5], rapid shallow breathing pattern [5, 6], and gradual increase in end-expiratory volume [6] that adversely affects their work of breathing [5-7]. Use of nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) levels of 6-7 cmH 2 O in this situation has been associated with rapid unloading of respiratory muscles, increased expiratory time, and concomitantly improved respiratory distress [5, 6, 8]. In comparison with historical cohorts supported exclusively by invasive ventilation, more recent studies have reported that first-line nCPAP also reduces duration of ventilation and hospital stay [9, 10]. Thus, the preemptive nCPAP strategy has been increasingly used over the last decade, and it is currently the gold-standard respiratory support for moderate to severe AVB [10].

The provision of CPAP requires specific equipment, trained teams, continuous monitoring, and a level of supervision that is usually found only in PICUs. Oxygen delivery with high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) allows the administration of a heated and humidified mixture of air and oxygen at a flow higher than the patient's inspiratory flow [11]. It has been widely adopted in PICUs and for interhospital transport of critically ill children, as the system is easily set up and is well tolerated by patients [12]. In the context of AVB, retrospective audits and observational studies have suggested promising outcomes on both physiological [7, 13] and clinical variables [14-18]. Two randomized controlled studies in infants not affected by a severe form of AVB reported efficiency comparable to that of hypertonic saline in treating respiratory distress signs [19] and a significant increase in SpO2 within the first 12 h of management compared with head-box oxygen therapy [20]. However, no study has yet provided a direct demonstration of HFNC efficacy and safety compared with the gold-standard respiratory support, nCPAP [21]. Given the effects of HFNC on the work of breathing and lung volumes [13, 22], the ease of installation, and the good tolerance [23], we hypothesized that this support would be an appropriate alternative to nCPAP. We performed a multicenter, randomized, noninferiority trial of HFNC compared with nCPAP for the initial respiratory management in young infants with moderate to severe AVB.
Methods
This prospective randomized multicenter trial was conducted in five PICUs from five French university hospital centers.
Ethical consideration

This study was conducted in accordance with the amended Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the South Mediterranean IV Ethics Committee (ID-RCB: 2014-A01029-38; 2014-09-09), and no amendment was made thereafter. This clinical trial was recorded in the National Library of Medicine registry (NCT 02457013; 2015-01-27).
Written authorization was obtained from the two parents. If one of the parents was absent, deferred signed authorization was accepted after a telephone call and oral agreement.
Population

Patients aged from 1 day to 6 months and hospitalized in the PICU were eligible for inclusion if the following conditions were all met: (1) clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis; (2) moderate to severe respiratory distress, defined by a modified Wood's clinical asthma score (mWCAS) >3; (3) no underlying cardiac or neuromuscular disease and no pneumothorax on chest radiograph; (4) absence of indication for imminent intubation; and (5) authorization to perform the study signed by both parents.
Study design

On admission, the nurse started monitoring the infant with pulse oximetry (SpO2), blood pressure, and transcutaneous CO2 (TcCO2). A mixture of air/oxygen was provided at a flow rate of 1 L/min, with FiO 2 set in order to reach SpO 2 of 94-97%. Corticosteroid, bronchodilator, and chest physiotherapy were stopped if provided beforehand. Chest X-ray and capillary blood gas measurements were performed, and the infant was maintained in a quiet environment. Baseline observation was made 15 min later to collect respiratory rate (RR), heart rate (HR), mWCAS [24], and neonatal pain and discomfort using the EDIN scale [25].
[DOCLING_PAGE 3]

When an infant met the inclusion criteria, respiratory support was randomly allocated as nCPAP or HFNC. Two different systems were used to generate nCPAP: the Infant Flow Ventilator (Electro Medical Equipment, Brighton, UK), and the FlexiTrunk infant interface (Fisher and Paykel, Villebon, France) connected to ventilator CPAP setups. Whatever the system, positive continuous pressure was set at + 7 cmH2O [6]. The sole HFNC device used was the Optiflow (Fisher and Paykel, Villebon France). Flow was delivered at 2 L/kg/min, with the device equipped with a pressure release valve set at 45 cmH2O. In both groups, FiO2 was titrated in order to achieve a normoxic SpO2 of 94-97%, as usually recommended in PICUs [10, 15, 26], and the humidifier was auto set at 37 °C.

The protocol lasted a minimum of 24 h after the allocated treatment had begun. In both groups, RR, HR, mWCAS, EDIN score, skin lesion score, FiO2, SpO2, and TcCO2 were systematically assessed 1 h, 12 h, and 24 h after the start of the procedure. Detailed information on the protocol was given to the nursing teams in each PICU to ensure that an investigator would be notified as soon as the continuous monitoring or scores indicated worsening in an infant's condition. At any moment during this period, occurrence of at least one failure criterion justified a switch to the alternative respiratory support. Patients switched from one group to the other were maintained on the second support for 24 h, and the data were again collected 1 h, 12 h, and 24 h following the crossover. A patient failing with the alternative respiratory support was maintained in the study, but the protocol was stopped and the next therapeutic step was decided by the physician involved in the patient's care.
Randomization and masking

Patients were centrally randomized to assign them to receive either nCPAP or HFNC. Randomization was performed using block sizes of two and four and was stratified by center. Randomization lists were prepared by the Clinical Research and Epidemiology Unit of Montpellier University Hospital. Allocations were concealed in opaque sealed envelopes.
Failure criteria

Failure was defined by the occurrence of one of the following criteria: (1) a 1-point increase in mWCAS compared with baseline; (2) RR rise >10 bpm compared with baseline, with RR >60 bpm; (3) a 1-point increase in the EDIN score compared with baseline, with EDIN >4 despite the use of hydroxyzine (1 mg/kg); and (4) more than two severe apnea episodes per hour (i.e., requiring bag and mask ventilation), despite a loading dose of caffeine (20 mg/kg) after the first apnea.
Outcome

The primary outcome was treatment failure within 24 h after randomization. This limited duration took into account (1) the policy in some participating PICUs of transferring stabilized patients after a few days and (2) several reports that the risk of failure is highest within 24 h of commencing the two techniques [16, 17, 27, 28]. Prespecified secondary outcomes included delay, causes, and predictors of failure [29], success rate after crossover, intubation rate, occurrence of skin lesions, length of stay, and serious adverse events (air leak syndrome and death).
Scales and scores

mWCAS is a composite score assessing the severity of bronchiolitis through five components: cyanosis, inspiratory breath sounds, accessory muscle use, expiratory wheezing, and cerebral function. Each is rated as follows: 0 for none, 0.5 for mild, 1 for moderate, and 2 for maximal [5]. A visual analog scale is used to standardize the scoring of accessory muscle use and wheezing [30].
EDIN is a neonatal pain and discomfort scale comprising five behavioral indicators: facial activity, body movements, quality of sleep, quality of contact, and consolability [25].
Skin lesions were documented according to the National Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel (NPUAP) definitions [31].
Statistical analyses

To satisfy the noninferiority criterion, we considered that the failure rate of the HFNC device should lie within 15% of the failure rate of the CPAP device. A power calculation indicated that 142 patients were needed for the study, using an estimated 85% success rate for both devices, power of 80%, and p < 0.05. This success rate was extrapolated from key studies using either of the two techniques [9, 10, 14-18, 27, 28]. The noninferiority of the HFNC device was assessed by the one-sided FarringtonManning confidence limit for the risk method using the prespecified noninferiority margin of 15%. Both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses were performed.

Results

From 1 November 2014 to 1 March 2015, 342 infants were admitted to the PICUs with a diagnosis of AVB. A total of 142 (77.6%) were included from the 183 eligible patients (Fig. 1). Twenty six (18%) had been born prematurely. Their postnatal age was comparable ( p = 0.21) but their weight was lower ( p < 0.001) than that of the other infants. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was positive for 125 (88%). Following randomization, patients-including those born preterm-were equally distributed into the CPAP and HFNC groups ( n = 71 in each, Table 1).
Primary endpoint
Failure occurred in 22 of 71 infants (31.0%) in the nCPAP group and 36 of 71 infants (50.7%) in the HFNC group.
Noninferiority analysis

With a risk-difference of -19% (95% CI -35 to -3%), the prespecified noninferiority margin of -15% was included in the confidence limit, not allowing the conclusion of noninferiority ( p = 0.707). Hence, the result allowed us to test the superiority of nCPAP compared with HFNC.

Superiority analysis

The intention-to-treat population was used to test the superiority of nCPAP compared with HFNC. With a difference of 20% (95% CI 4-36%), success was higher in the nCPAP group ( p = 0.001), suggesting the superiority of nCPAP and a relative risk of success 1.63 (95% CI 1.022.63) higher with nCPAP compared with HFNC.
Secondary endpoints
Timing and causes of failure

Sixty percent of failures (35/58) were observed during the first 6 h following treatment allocation (Fig. 2). The mean time to failure was comparable between groups [6.7 (5.7) vs 9.7 (8.8) h, p = 0.19].

The reasons for treatment failure in the two study groups were rise in m-WCAS (31 cases), rise in RR (27 cases), rise in EDIN score (19 cases), and apnea (7 cases). Discomfort was the leading cause of failure in the nCPAP group. Worsening of respiratory distress signs was more frequent in the HFNC group (Table 2).

Prespecified patient's outcomes
All patients who failed were switched to the alternative respiratory support (Fig. 3). The success rate with the alternative support did not differ between groups ( p = 0.53).

The main prespecified data collected after the protocol was revealed no significant difference between groups (Table 3). Eight (5.7%) infants were intubated during PICU hospitalization. Two, both randomized into the HFNC group, were intubated during the protocol period, and six after its completion. Three of them had been randomized into the nCPAP group, including one switched to HFNC. The three others had been randomized into the HFNC group and were all switched to nCPAP. Intubation tended to be associated with HFNC failure ( p = 0.054) but not with nCPAP failure ( p = 1).
