2.4. Chest physiotherapy and mist-steam
While there is insufficient evidence to show any benefit of mist-steam in bronchiolitis [9], chest physiotherapy has proved ineffective [8].
2.5. Hypertonic saline

In recent years, a growing body of literature has supported the use of nebulized hypertonic saline (HS). The mechanisms of its action are well described in the paper by Mandelberg and Amirav [30], and include a reduction in airway edema, a greater mucus clearance and less viscous secretions. Studies investigating the usefulness of 3% HS have been conducted in the past 10 years and have included both outpatients and inpatients. Recent reviews [7,31,32] have highlighted a divergence between the results of studies conducted on already hospitalized patients (for whom HS was found to reduce the hospital stay) and studies that included emergency department patients (using HS was not effective in reducing the hospital admission rate, although it coincided with a transient improvement in clinical severity score). These results support the hypothesis that HS is useful when delivered repeatedly and assessed in terms of longer-term outcomes, but less so as a single dose and with short-term outcome.

Despite the lack of strong evidence to recommend the routine use of HS for the treatment of bronchiolitis, its high safety profile, low cost and non-invasive administration make it a reasonable option for treating children with bronchiolitis. A recent article by Ralston and colleagues [33] showed that it is safe even when administered alone without salbutamol, refuting previous concerns that administering HS could trigger bronchospasm and should be given together with bronchodilators. Only one study so far has evaluated the usefulness of 5% HS, finding a good safety profile and a greater effectiveness than with normal saline, but no difference compared with 3% HS [32,34].

Several randomized controlled trials are currently underway on the effectiveness of HS in bronchiolitis and will soon provide better evidence to support strong recommendations on its use (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/results?term=hypertonic+ saline+AND+bronchiolitis&pg=2).
3. Pharmacological therapy
3.1. Beta-agonists

The results of two recent systematic reviews [10,11] showed that nebulized bronchodilators are ineffective in the treatment of bronchiolitis, supporting the recommendations of previous guidelines [5,6,27]. Bronchodilators are unable to improve oxygen saturation, the hospital admission rate, the length of hospital stays, or the time to recovery at home.
The mild improvement in clinical scores associated with the use of bronchodilators has to be balanced against the risk of their side effects and their cost.
3.2. Adrenaline

According to the most recent available evidence, nebulized adrenaline seems to be the only pharmacological therapy showing some effectiveness in the treatment of bronchiolitis. Administering adrenaline has revealed positive effects on shortterm measures, improving the clinical score and reducing admission rates in the first 24 hours of care. No benefits have been observed for inpatients, however [11,12,35]. Given the shortage of studies and its potential adverse effects, adrenaline is not recommended in the home setting [5].
3.3. Steroids

Both systemic and inhaled steroids have been amply investigated as a treatment for bronchiolitis. The results of these studies have recently been summarized in high-quality systematic reviews and meta-analyses [11,13,14]. No clinically relevant effects of either systemic or inhaled steroids were found in terms of admission rates or length of hospitalization. In addition, inhaled steroids given during the acute phase of bronchiolitis have had no effect in preventing post-bronchiolitis wheezing [14].
3.4. Combinations of adrenaline and steroids

The Canadian multicenter randomized double-blind, placebocontrolled trial recently published by Plint and colleagues [36] was the first to find a positive effect of a combined therapy with nebulized adrenaline and oral dexamethasone. However, the very high doses of dexamethasone (1mg/kg followed by 0.6 mg/kg for the next 5 days) and the prolonged treatment in this young age group raise concern as regards the possible long-term effects on the child's neurocognitive development, given the lack of data on the combination's long-term safety. In addition, this study was not initially planned to specifically investigate the effects of the combination of adrenaline and dexamethasone, so it was not adequately powered for this analysis and the results failed to reach statistical significance when the adjusted analysis was performed. Even the biological plausibility of the efficacy of such a combined therapy remains to be clarified [35].
3.5. Antibiotics

The use of antibiotics in children with bronchiolitis has long been discussed. The guidelines recommend antibiotics only when a bacterial co-infection is identified or highly likely [5,6,27]. A recent Cochrane review [37] found only minimal evidence to support the use of antibiotics in bronchiolitis, and called for further research to identify subgroups of patients (i.e. patients with chronic lung disease, hemodynamically significant heart disease, hospitalized in intensive care) who might benefit most from the use of antibiotics.

It has also been suggested that macrolides may be useful in treating bronchiolitis because of their anti-inflammatory immunomodulatory effect. Previous studies generated conflicting results [38,39], however, and the most recent randomized controlled trial found no benefit of macrolides in children with bronchiolitis, recommending against their use, given that overuse increases overall antibiotic resistance [40].

According to a recent Cochrane review [41] there are insufficient data to provide reliable estimates on its effects in bronchiolitis. Given uncertainty about its effectiveness and the lack of data on its safety, this treatment option might be considered only for children with severe disease, or underlying conditions that predispose them to more severe presentation, such as immunodeficiencies, chronic lung disease or haemodynamically significant heart diseases [5].
3.7. Other pharmacological options

Although high leukotriene concentrations have been found in the respiratory secretions of children with bronchiolitis, suggesting a pathogenic role of these mediators in bronchiolitis [42], conflicting results have been reported on the effectiveness of antileukotriene medication such as montelukast, and no systematic reviews on the topic have been published so far [43,44]. Even the possible role of montelukast in preventing recurrent respiratory symptoms after bronchiolitis remains to be clarified [45-48].

Conflicting results have also emerged on the use of nebulized DNase - believed to improve airway clearance of secretions thanks to its mucolytic properties [49-51] - and the latest Cochrane review does not support its use in children with bronchiolitis [15].
Only one study has investigated the use of nebulized furosemide, which was found ineffective [52].

As for RSV bronchiolitis-associated apneas, only case series have shown a benefit of methylxanthines, such as caffeine and theophylline, as a consequence of their central respiratory stimulant effect [53,54], while most severe cases may need ventilatory support. However, even though epidemiological data on the prevalence of this condition are lacking [55], any evidence of the effectiveness of medical treatment will have a significant impact on the treatment of young infants, who more often present with RSV-related apneas.
4. Future therapeutic perspectives

It has recently been shown in both animal models and adult humans infected with RSV, that antiviral therapy based on RNA interference may be an effective treatment for bronchiolitis [56]. RNA interference is a natural mechanism regulating protein expression that is mediated by small interfering RNAs. Intranasal administration of small interfering RNA targeting specific RSV gene expression may change the approach to the treatment of bronchiolitis in the future [57].
5. Prevention/prophylaxis
The absence of an effective treatment for bronchiolitis makes prevention the best choice to reduce the burden of the disease and its impact on social health [3].

In recent years, immunoprophylaxis with palivizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody capable of neutralizing RSV, has proved effective in reducing hospitalization rates relating to RSV infections [58-60]. This prophylaxis cannot be offered to the whole population of children under 24 months of age because of its high cost. The current recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) for the management of bronchiolitis identify specific groups of children found to benefit from prophylaxis with palivizumab (Table 2) and the minimal number of doses needed to guarantee an effective protection [5,61].

Other groups of high-risk patients who could benefit from palivizumab prophylaxis, i.e. children with cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiencies, have recently been evaluated in different studies and palivizumab has proved safe and effective in these children as well [62,63].

It is important not to forget that, although RSV accounts for the majority of cases, it is not the only virus implicated in bronchiolitis. General prevention strategies to combat the risk factors, as well as parent and caregiver education, must therefore remain the first line of intervention for clinicians [2]. Frequent handwashing, avoiding exposing children to tobacco smoke [64], and breastfeeding have proved very effective in protecting infants and children against lower respiratory tract infections (and RSVrelated ones in particular) [2,5].

An interesting field in the prevention of bronchiolitis concerns the relationship between respiratory viral infections and vitamin D. A deficiency of vitamin D has been seen to increase the risk of viral respiratory tract infections and RSV-associated bronchiolitis [65]. A recent prospective birth cohort study demonstrated that children who are vitamin D deficient at birth have a six-fold risk of developing RSV bronchiolitis in the first year of life [66]. These preliminary data suggest that action to change the vitamin D status of mothers during pregnancy and/or vitamin D supplementation of infants could reduce the risk of RSV-associated bronchiolitis.
6. Conclusion

In summary, available evidence shows that administering oxygen and clearing the upper airways of secretions is still the mainstay of treatment for bronchiolitis. HFNC oxygen delivery seems a promising non-invasive mode of respiratory support, but further studies are needed to better define its role in the treatment of children with bronchiolitis outside the intensive care setting. Nasogastric feeding has proved safe and just as effective as intravenous fluid administration. Hypertonic saline seems to be effective in reducing the hospital stay for inpatients, while mist-steam and chest physiotherapy appear to have no role in treating bronchiolitis.

Of the pharmacological options, nebulized adrenaline is the only medication found to be effective in reducing admission rates in the first 24 hours after assessment at the emergency department, but there is still no evidence of its usefulness for inpatients. The available data on the effectiveness of combining adrenaline with high doses of dexamethasone cannot support the routine use of this treatment option and only further studies could clarify its real efficacy and long-term effects.
The intranasal administration of antiviral therapy based on RNA interference may change the therapeutic approach to bronchiolitis in the future.
Immunoprophylaxis with palivizumab remains the recommended prevention therapy for children at high risk of severe bronchiolitis.
Vitamin D may help to prevent respiratory tract infections, but further studies are needed to better clarify its role in bronchiolitis prophylaxis.

Comparison of a high-flow humidified nasal cannula to nasal continuous positive airway pressure in children with acute bronchiolitis: experience in a pediatric intensive care unit
Prune Metge & Céline Grimaldi & Sophie Hassid &
Laurent Thomachot & Anderson Loundou & Claude Martin & Fabrice Michel
Received: 26 November 2013 /Revised: 6 January 2014 /Accepted: 22 January 2014 /Published online: 14 February 2014 # Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2014

Abstract The objective of the current study is to compare the use of a nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) to a high-flow humidified nasal cannula (HFNC) in infants with acute bronchiolitis, who were admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) during two consecutive seasons. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of all infants admitted to a PICU at a tertiary care French hospital during the bronchiolitis seasons of 2010/11 and 2011/12. Infants admitted to the PICU, who required noninvasive respiratory support, were included. The first noninvasive respiratory support modality was nCPAP during the 2010/11 season, while HFNC was used during the 2011/2012 season. We compared the length of stay (LOS) in the PICU; the daily measure of PCO2 and pH; and the mean of the five higher values of heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), FiO2, and SpO2 each day, during the first 5 days. Thirty-four children met the inclusion criteria: 19 during the first period (nCPAP group) and 15 during the second period (HFNC group). Parameters such as LOS in PICU and oxygenation were similar in the two groups. Oxygen weaning occurred during the same time for the two groups. There were no differences between the two groups for RR, HR, FiO2, and CO2 evolution. HFNC therapy failed in three patients, two of whom required invasive mechanical

Conclusion : We did not find a difference between HFNC and nCPAP in the management of severe bronchiolitis in our PICU. Larger prospective studies are required to confirm these findings.
Keywords Acute viral bronchiolitis . Respiratory distress . Nasal CPAP . High-flow nasal cannula
Introduction

In acute viral bronchiolitis, distal airway obstruction reduces dynamic pulmonary compliance and increases the expiratory time, creating an intrinsically positive-end expiratory pressure [2, 7, 10]. In the most severe cases, respiratory failure occurs, associated with hypercapnia, hypoxia, and apneic syndrome. Hospitalization in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can therefore be required for respiratory support treatment [5].

Several studies have demonstrated the efficacy of nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP), by reducing the clinical signs of respiratory distress, the work of breathing, hypercapnia, the need for tracheal intubation as well as reducing complications of invasive ventilation [2, 5, 7, 8, 13, 17, 19].

Recently, high-flow humidified nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy has been tested for the management of acute respiratory failure in adults and children [6, 9, 14]. It delivers heated, humidified gas with a constantly higher flow than a standard cannula. It allows constant FiO2 of inspired gas, washes out the dead space, and provides a variable level of positive airway pressure (depending on several parameters [6, 9]). Its use is rapidly growing in neonatal intensive care units (NICU), because it is easier, better tolerated, associated with less nasal trauma, and has a lower cost compared to that of the usual CPAP devices [4, 21]. Some authors have shown that its use in acute viral bronchiolitis management can also reduce respiratory rate (RR), PCO2, and intubation rate; however, failure of this treatment in the PICU could occur in more than 20 % of cases [1, 15].
[DOCLING_PAGE 2]

Data comparing nCPAP to HFNC in infants with acute viral bronchiolitis are limited [12, 20]. In 2011, we transitioned from the use of nCPAP to HFNC as a noninvasive respiratory support in infants with acute bronchiolitis as well as acute respiratory failure, prior to use of invasive mechanical ventilation. As stated, the objective of the current study is to compare the use of nCPAP to HFNC as noninvasive respiratory support systems in infants with acute bronchiolitis admitted to the PICU during two consecutive seasons.
Materials and methods
We conducted a retrospective study of infants admitted to our tertiary center ' s PICU during two consecutive seasons of acute bronchiolitis: the winters of 2010/11 and 2011/12.

The noninvasive respiratory support used during the 2010/11 season was nCPAP. In September 2011, we transitioned from nCPAP to HFNC as the modality of choice for noninvasive respiratory support in infants with acute bronchiolitis admitted to the PICU.
The ethics committee waived the need for consent in this retrospective review of medical records, which is congruent with French law.
Patients

Infants with acute bronchiolitis, and one of or more of the following, were eligible for inclusion in the study: (1) oxygen requirement to maintain SpO2>92 %, (2) hypercarbia PCO2> 50 mmHg, (3) acidosis pH<7.30, and (4) apnea. Infants who needed tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation at the time of admission to the PICU, however, were excluded.
Respiratory support

According to our guidelines during the first period (2010/11), infants needing respiratory support were initially treated with nCPAP (Infant Flow, Viasys Healthcare Inc., Yorba Linda, CA, USA). The positive airway pressure objective was 4 to 6 cm H2O. If failure did occur with this treatment, pressure support noninvasive ventilation or tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation were initiated, according to the clinical judgment of the physician in charge. During the second period (2011/12), the protocol was modified and the initial respiratory support was replaced by HFNC, using a heated humidified high-flow delivery system (RT329 System with the MR850 humidifier, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand) and connected to an oxygen therapy nasal cannula (BC2745 and BC2755, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand). The nasal prong size was selected according to the manufacturer ' s recommendations, while the system was equipped with a pressure release valve set at 45 cm H2O.

Initial flow rate was set at 1 L/kg/min during the first hour, though, it could be increased by 1 L/kg/min (up to 3 L/kg/min without exceeding 8 L/min) if the initial clinical status did not improve, as per the physician in charge ' s evaluation of the patient. In the event of worsened clinical or blood gas parameters or a need for FiO2>40 %, despite maximal flow, HFNC was replaced by nCPAP and failure of treatment was considered. Similar to the first period, failure of nCPAP treatment was assessed by the physician in charge and could be switched for noninvasive mechanical ventilation or tracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation.

In both periods, monitoring included heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and SpO2 continuous recording. HR, RR, SPO2, and FiO2 were noted every hour. Noninvasive arterial pressure was also measured every hour as well. Capillary blood gas analysis (RAPIDLab 1265, Siemens, Munich, Germany) was performed on admission, and then at a minimum of once a day, by heel puncture using capillary tubes. All infants had peripheral venous catheters with glucose infusion for the first day. Continuous enteral nutrition was introduced at 20 ml/kg/h by an orogastric tube on the first day, and then progressively increased.

Weaning from respiratory support was the same for both techniques and was started once the FiO2<25 % and the PCO2<45 mmHg. Respiratory support was replaced by lowflow nasal cannula (1 L/min). FiO2 was adapted to maintain SpO2>90 %. In the case of weaning failure (based on clinical judgment or SpO2<90 % with FiO2 100 %), noninvasive respiratory support was restarted and then stopped the next day.
Data

The following information was extracted from the patient ' s medical records: age, gender, weight, location prior to PICU admission, positive or negative respiratory syncytial virus detected by PCR in nasal secretions, HR, RR, FiO2, pH, and PCO2 at admission. The mean of the five higher values of HR, RR, and FiO2 for each day and the first daily measure of pH and PCO2 were recorded for the first 5 days of PICU hospitalization. Data collection was stopped in the case of respiratory support treatment modification (a switch to CPAP when the infant was treated by HFNC or intubation when the infant was treated by nCPAP), which included respiratory support weaning. All treatment complications were also recorded.
[DOCLING_PAGE 3]
Statistical analysis

Data are expressed as medians (25e -75e percentile) and percentages, with parametric statistics also employed. Comparisons between groups at the time of admission were assessed using Student ' s t test or chi-2 test. HR, RR, FiO2, and PCO2 evolutions were compared between the two groups with a two-way analysis of variance for repeated measures. The statistical analyses were performed with the SPSS software package version 17.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Statistical significance was defined as p <0.05.
Results

Thirty-four infants were included in the analysis: 19 for the first period (2010/11; nCPAP group), 15 for the second period (2011/12; HFNC group). Age, gender, weight at admission, RSV status, location prior to PICU admission, and hospital length of stay before PICU admission were similar between the two groups (Table 1).

Both groups were similar for pH, PCO2, and oxygen saturation at admission and for maximal HR, RR, and FiO2 during the first day in the PICU. Length of stay in the PICU was not statistically different between the two groups (Table 1). Two infants in the HFNC group had comorbidities: one had a history of severe prematurity (28 SA) with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and the second had Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

Treatment failure occurred in one infant in the nCPAP group on day 2. He was intubated because of respiratory exhaustion, along with severe respiratory acidosis (pH 7.08, PCO2 76 mmHg), which was responsible for somnolence and global hypotonia. In the HFNC group, treatment failure occurred in three patients on day 2, so that treatment was switched to nCPAP. Clinical improvement was observed for one of them, while the two others required intubation and mechanical ventilation for less than 12 h after treatment modification.

Multivariate analysis for repeated measures showed a difference in evolution of the mean maximal HR from day 1 to day 5 in the two groups ( p <0.01), but there was no difference in HR between groups (Fig. 1).

Mean maximal RR decreased significantly in the two groups from day 1 to day 5 ( p <0.01), but there was no difference of the RR between the two groups (Fig. 1). PCO2 significantly decreased in both groups from day 1 to day 5 ( p <0.01), with a trend to lower values in the HFNC group, although the difference did not reach statistical significance ( p =0.051) (Fig. 1).

Mean maximal FiO2 decreased constantly in the two groups ( p <0.01) after use of noninvasive respiratory support, without a significant difference between groups. Oxygen weaning was accomplished during the same time for both groups (Fig. 2).
The mean pH significantly increased in the two groups over time ( p <0.001), without any difference observed between them (Fig. 1). No treatment complications were noted in the two groups.

Discussion

We compared two groups of infants treated with nCPAP or HFNC for acute viral bronchiolitis in the PICU. We did not find any difference between groups for respiratory parameters or length of stay in the PICU, suggesting that HFNC is as efficient as nCPAP in improving respiratory distress in infants with acute bronchiolitis.

The two groups in our study were similar at the time of PICU admission. Pediatric index mortality 2 (PIM 2) and length of stay in the PICU are concordant with previous reports [2, 7, 15]. The management of acute viral bronchiolitis is well codified in our unit, and except for respiratory support, none of the treatments was added or modified between the two seasons. In particular, there was no need for nebulized bronchodilatator or corticosteroid treatment, and as such, we

believe that HFNC was as efficient as nCPAP. This result is in accordance with a recent randomized study, which also found no difference between the two devices in preventing reintubation in preterm neonates [3].

Similar to nCPAP, HFNC is known to provide positive-end expiratory pressure. In patients with moderate respiratory distress, due to acute viral bronchiolitis, HFNC with a flow of 2 L/kg/min develops a relevant pharyngeal pressure, thereby reducing respiratory effort by 50 % and improving clinical status [16]. In 18 preterm infants, using HFNC at 3, 4, and 5 L/ min flow allowed for decreased work of breathing as well as using nCPAP at 6 cm H2O pressure [18]. In our study, oxygenation parameters were identical in the two groups and improved in the same manner. Although the difference was not significant, we observed higher FiO2 in the HFNC group during the first 2 days, despite equal FiO 2 on admission. Three children in the HFNC group required a switch in treatment to nCPAP, and two were intubated. Clinical deterioration occurred in the first 24 h after admission, while intubation was performed on day 2. The positive-end expiratory pressure (PEEP) delivered with HFNC depends on the flow, diameter of the nasal prongs relative to the nostrils, and gas leaks by mouth. Therefore, PEEP level remains uncertain and possibly time-varying [11, 16], unlike the Instant Flow SiPAP system, which provides stable PEEP. This variability in PEEP level could be responsible for temporary alveolar derecruitment, leading to respiratory worsening.

Afavorable effect on hypercapnia was also observed in the two groups. This effect has been widely reported with nCPAP [2, 19], but only one study reported PCO2 improvement with HFNCinacute viral bronchiolitis [13]. Interestingly, we found a trend that lowers PCO2 in the HFNC group. One explanation for this is an important wash out of dead space with HFNC [6, 9]. Greater improvement could also be linked to better tolerance of HFNC. Indeed, nCPAP requires a hermetic nasal mask, which is difficult to install and maintain in place. It affects points of high pressure on the face and could be responsible for pain, discomfort, and at times cutaneous necrosis [3]. Resulting agitation can impair gas exchange, hence CO2 removal. Nonresponders to HFNC have recently been studied as well [1]. Higher PCO2 and lower RR on admission were associated with HFNC failure; however, in our two cases, these criteria were not present.

Several limitations of our study must be mentioned. The samples sizes are small, thus limiting the value of our findings, insofar as small variations cannot be shown. Apnea occurrence, clinical scores, and the exact conditions of nasal prong use are not available in a retrospective study. For example, use of a pacifier reduces mouth air leaks and could have impacted treatment efficiency [16]. Another problem was that treatment failure was not clearly defined, but left to the clinical judgment of the physician in charge. Finally, it is important to note that the population of this study was predominantly very young infants; as a result, the findings could not be extended to older children.
Conclusion

In this study comparing HFNC to nCPAP for severe acute viral bronchiolitis in infants, we observed no difference in the length of stay in the PICU, respiratory rate, PCO2, FiO2, and duration of oxygen support. These results should encourage further investigation in order to more comprehensively compare respiratory supports in a larger, controlled prospective evaluation.

REVIEW
High flow nasal cannula in the emergency department: indications, safety and effectiveness
Justin Wang a , Khai Pin Lee b , Shu-Ling Chong b , Mervin Loi c and Jan Hau Lee c

a Paediatric Intensive Care Unit, Royal Brompton Hospital, London, UK; b Children ' s Emergency, KK Women ' s and Children ' s Hospital, Singapore, Singapore; c Children ' s Intensive Care Unit, KK Women ' s and Children ' s Hospital, Singapore, Singapore
ABSTRACT

Introduction : Heated humidified high flow nasal cannula therapy (HHHFNCT) is emerging as a popular non-invasive mode of respiratory support in adults and children. In recent years, its use has extended beyond the intensive care unit to other clinical areas. This review aims to explore the mechanism of action, indications, safety, and effectiveness of HHHFNCT use in the Emergency Department (ED).
Areas covered : The mechanism of action of HHHFNCT, as well as its use in adult and pediatric ED will be discussed in this review.

Expert commentary : While there exists increasing enthusiasm in the use of HHHFNCT in the ED, constant monitoring of the patients and an experienced assessment of their response to treatment are critical and may require additional manpower deployment, which may be challenging, in the busy ED environment. Our experience with the use of HHHFNCT in children is still growing. Continual research in this area remains crucial in helping us better understand the patient types and conditions managed in ED that would most benefit from this device.
1. Introduction

Heated humidified high flow nasal cannula therapy (HHHFNCT) has surfaced as an important means of delivering humidified oxygen and offers an alternative non-invasive mode of ventilatory support for adults and children in respiratory distress [1]. The physiological benefits include the reduction in rebreathing as the nasopharyngeal dead space is constantly being replaced with fresh oxygen at high flow rates, and the increase in the amount of oxygen delivered given a reduction in entrained room air [2]. In contrast, conventional non-invasive ventilation (NIV) increases dead space due to the interfaces used [3]. Although high end-expiratory pressure cannot be generated since the circuit is open, some degree of positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) is created [4] which is important in preventing atelectasis. In normal spontaneous breathing, the upper airway has the ability to humidify and warm air even if the air is dry and cold [5]. However, supplemental oxygen is not warm and humidified at low flow, and in a long run would result in nose and mouth dryness. In essence, due to warm moist gas being delivered, HHHFNCT is better tolerated, and for the same reason, mucociliary function is maintained and improves mucosal toileting in the setting of inflammatory response from different causes. Clinical applications for HHHFNCT among adults include hypoxemic respiratory failure, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, post-operative, post-extubation, and palliative respiratory support [6]. HHHFNCT has also been reported to reduce the effort of breathing among children with bronchiolitis, pneumonia, asthma, and obstructive sleep apnea [7 -10]. Previously, the

use of HHHFNCT was confined to the adult, neonatal and pediatric intensive care and high dependency units [11 -14]. However, in recent years, there has been a growing trend in its utilization in the emergency department (ED). Although there has been a number of randomized control trials (RCT) of the use of HHHFNCT in adults in the ED [15 -17], there remains a limited number of such trials conducted in the pediatric emergency medicine setting [18]. A review on the indications, safety, and effectiveness of HHHFNCT within the ED setting is timely. Where pertinent, we included some important animal studies to describe in greater detail the mechanisms of action of HHHFNCT in the support of patients with respiratory distress.
2. Methods

We performed a Medline search using the following keywords and/or MESH terms: high flow nasal cannula, oxygen inhalation therapy, positive pressure respiration, nasal cannula, nasal prong, and emergency service. We also hand searched relevant publications from articles obtained from the above search strategy. In this clinical review, we excluded nonEnglish publications and abstracts.
3. Mechanisms of action of HHHFNCT
HHHFNCT aims to deliver an air and oxygen admixture at a flow rate that exceeds the patient ' s inspiratory flow requirements [19]. There are several putative mechanisms of action for HHHFNCT.

3.1. Nasopharyngeal dead space ' wash-out '

One of the suggested mechanisms of action for HHHFNCT is that it provides gas at a flow rate that replaces the nasopharyngeal space with fresh gas, thereby reducing the effects of rebreathing [2]. A study using a silicone resin model of the human nasal cavity showed that HHHFNCT flushes out the dead space in the nasal cavity, with turbulent mixing contributing to carbon dioxide clearance [20].

Additional supporting evidence was provided by an animal study using neonatal piglets with lung injury [21]. Comparison was made between Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) and HHHFNCT, with further subdivision of the HHHFNCT cohort into either high or low leak as determined by the type of nasal prong provided. Analysis of the results in the HHHFNCT subgroup showed that increasing HHHFNCT flow, under both leak conditions, resulted in improved partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) and oxygen (PaO2) in a manner which was independent of tracheal pressure alone. This improvement in gas exchange with increasing HHHFNCT flow continued up till a certain point, beyond which subsequent increments in flow rates no longer had any impact -the so-called ' saturation point ' . Furthermore, the piglets receiving HHHFNCT via the prongs with high leak had lower PaCO2 at flow rates <6 L/min than both the low leak or CPAP groups, suggesting that nasopharyngeal washout was a significant factor in gas exchange. In contrast, there was no incremental change in PaCO2 and PaO2 with increasing CPAP pressure [21]. Other studies using tracheal gas insufflation have also shown that gas exchange plateaus with increasing gas flow, when presumably washout of the dead space is maximal [22]. Collectively, these findings support the theory that washout of the nasopharyngeal dead space at least partly explains the effects seen with HHHFNCT. Extrathoracic dead space per kilogram of body weight decreases exponentially with increasing age in young children, and is up to three times greater in young infants compared to adults [23]. This suggests that the effect of dead space wash out is likely to be even greater in younger children.
3.2. Increased capacity for oxygen delivery

The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) delivered by conventional low-flow devices is inaccurate and often much less than predicted [24,25], with the notable exception of Venturi masks [26]. Additionally, the minute ventilation in healthy adults has been shown to range from 30 L/min when performing light work, up to 70 L/min when performing heavy work [27]. Since conventional means of delivering supplementary oxygen are generally accepted to be limited to 15L/min, the maximum inspiratory flow rate of patients in acute respiratory distress is likely to outstrip delivery. This results in entrainment of room air, thereby effectively diluting the FiO2 that reaches the patient. HHHFNCT circumvents this by aiming to provide gas flow at a rate closer to maximum inspiratory flow rate, and has been shown in hypopharyngeal oxygraphy studies to deliver more accurate levels of FiO2 compared to low flow oxygen devices [28].
3.3. Generation of PEEP

Providing PEEP is fundamental to NIV techniques. It has been postulated that PEEP might also play a role in HHHFNCT therapy. Studies have shown that HHHFNCT can be used to generate PEEP of up to 12cmH2O in adults receiving gas flow of 100L/min [29]. PEEP generated is significantly higher in subjects who have their mouths closed than those who have their mouths open [30]. A prospective study was conducted in 15 adult patients post-cardiac surgery to compare the nasopharyngeal airway pressures generated by HHHFNCT and standard facemask therapy at 35 L/min of gas flow. This study showed that HHHFNCT generated a mean nasopharyngeal airway pressure of 2.7 [standard deviation (SD) 1.1] cmH2O when patients had their mouths closed, and 1.2 (SD 0.8) cmH2O with their mouths open [31]. The patients who received standard facemask therapy had negligible increase in nasopharyngeal airway pressure [31]. Other factors that may impact PEEP delivered by HHHFNCT include body mass index [32], gender [30], nasal prong fit [21] and leak around the nares [29].

Compared to the adult population, there are limited data for the amount of PEEP delivered by HHHFNCT in children. In a study of infants under 6 months old with acute Respiratory Syncytial Virus-positive bronchiolitis, pharyngeal pressure with HHHFNCT at flow rates of 2L/kg/min averaged approximately 4cmH2O, with good correlation between pharyngeal pressure and flow rate [33]. Generated PEEP can, however, be unpredictable in neonates receiving HHHFNCT, with one study showing that clinically significant CPAP could only be achieved in patients ≤ 1500 grams in weight and who had their mouths fully closed [34]. There is also likely to be substantial interand intra-individual variability in PEEP generated [35].

The measurement of end-expiratory lung impedance using electrical impedance tomography has been shown to reliably quantify lung volume changes [36]. This technique has demonstrated increased end expiratory lung volume in subjects receiving HHHFNCT [30], with a direct correlation to airway pressure generated [32]. This may reduce atelectasis and aid lung recruitment, thereby improving ventilation-perfusion matching and alveolar ventilation [19,37].
3.4. Effect on respiratory mechanics

Providing adequate heated humidified high-flow oxygen has been shown in various studies to reduce inspiratory resistance and work of breathing. First, by providing gas flows that are the same or exceeds the patient ' s peak inspiratory pressure, nasopharyngeal collapse that normally occurs during spontaneous respiration is counteracted, thereby decreasing upper airway resistance [2,38]. Second, warm and moist gas has been shown to improve mucociliary function which would maintain mucus clearance and prevent airway resistance and atelectasis [39]. Cold and dry gas can result in bronchoconstriction [40]. In vitro studies have also shown that exposure to low humidity conditions can exacerbate the inflammatory response of airway epithelial cells in humans [39]. HHHFNCT has also been noted to change the respiratory pattern of breathing. A study involving 38 adults showed an association of commencing HHHFNCT with reduction in respiratory rate, even though there was no statistically significant decrease in PaCO2 [41]. The investigators also found diminished thoracoabdominal asynchrony and dyspnea score as early as 15 minutes after initiating HHHFNCT, resulting in improved ventilation [41].

3.5. Improved tolerability

A number of studies have demonstrated better comfort and less mouth dryness with the use of HHHFNCT compared to standard oxygen therapy delivered by masks, most likely attributed to the warm and moist air generated. A visual analog scale was utilized to evaluate mouth dryness in a blinded study involving 20 patients, which expectedly showed a significant reduction of this when HHHFNCT was used [42]. In children with respiratory distress from various etiologies, a study using the COMFORT scale revealed an improvement in patient comfort when oxygen was delivered using the HHHFNCT system as opposed to via nasal cannula or face mask [43]. To a certain degree, the ability to be able to eat and speak easily may have contributed to this comfort perception. A neonatal study has shown that parents preferred HHHFNCT compared to CPAP as it was easier to interact with them and take part in their cares, although there was no significant difference in patient comfort as per the EDIN (neonatal pain and comfort) score [44]. A survey among clinical staff demonstrated that they found HHHFNCT to be easier to administer and believe that it was more comfortable for infants [45]. Nevertheless, there have also been a few reports of discomfort when using HHHFNCT (e.g. feeling hot, noisy, injury to the nasal mucosa, and displacement of the nasal cannula) [46].
4. HHHFNCT in the adult emergency department

Among adults with acute respiratory failure, the use of HHHFNCT was reported to be associated with better oxygenation, lower respiratory rate, and better tolerability when compared to NIV [42,47,48]. HHHFNCT may also be effective in reducing dyspnea in cardiogenic pulmonary edema [49].

HHHFNCT use in clinical practice has extended beyond the intensive care setting to the ED. In a prospective observation study, Lenglet et al. studied 17 patients with acute respiratory failure presenting to the ED, 9 of whom had pneumonia and 4 had cardiogenic pulmonary edema [50]. HHHFNCT was instituted at a median flow of 40L/min. Dyspnea scores improved as early as 15 min post HHHFNCT, oxygenation improved and respiratory rates decreased. This beneficial effect persisted through 60 minutes postHHHFNCT. Importantly, 82% of caregivers report that the patient was more comfortable with HHHFNCT, and 76% of healthcare staff preferred HHHFNCT over conventional oxygen therapy [50]. In a retrospective chart review of 81 patients in the ED, in whom the most common cause of respiratory failure was acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, arterial blood gas taken 2.4 ± 1.5 h after starting HHHFNCT revealed a significant reduction in PaCO2 levels from 54.7 ± 26.4 mmHg to 51.3 ± 25.8 mmHg among all patients ( p = 0.02) [51]. In a RCT in the ED of 40 patients, HHHFNCT significantly improved dyspnea and patient comfort when compared to conventional oxygen therapy, with no serious adverse events [52]. The HOT-ER study was an RCT of 303 adults presenting to the ED with hypoxia and tachypnea [16]. Patients were randomized to either HHHFNCT or to standard oxygen therapy. They found no statistically significant difference in conversion to mechanical ventilation in the ED between both groups [3.6% (95% CI 1.5 -7.9%) in the HHHFNCT group versus 7.2% (95% CI 3.8 -13%) in the standard oxygen therapy group ( p = 0.16)], and no difference in the length of stay in the ED (or in the hospital), or 90-day mortality. The authors did, however, highlighted the main limitation being the failure to reach the required sample size. Moreover, hypoxic patients that were not selected for the trial and the low rate of escalation to NIV could have biased the results to null [16]. In view of the limited ED trials, we describe the findings of a multicenter, open-label trial in intensive care units (ICUs) among 310 adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure [47]. The findings of this study may inform the impact of HHHFNCT on patients presenting with acute respiratory distress in the ED setting. Similar to the HOT-ER study [16], treatment with high-flow oxygen, standard oxygen therapy or NIV did not reveal any significant difference in intubation rates. However, there was a significant difference in 90-day mortality in favor of HHHFNCT compared with standard oxygen therapy (hazard ratio 2.01, 95% CI 1.01 -3.99). Although the choice of noninvasive respiratory support depends on the severity of hypoxemia, the role of NIV and HHHFNCT in this situation is still far from clear [53].

In summary, HHHFNCT appears to reduce dyspnea and tachypnea in patients with a wide range of respiratory diseases and is safe for use among adult patients in the ED. Whether the institution of HHHFNCT results in a lower rate of mechanical ventilation and long-term improved outcomes remains to be seen. Concerns have been expressed at extrapolating results of the current HHHFNCT studies to a largely variable ED patient population [54]. Delays in recognizing patient deterioration must be avoided. In the absence of a significant decrease in respiratory rate, poor oxygenation or persistent thoracoabdominal asynchrony after HHHFNCT initiation, clinicians must suspect possible HHHFNCT failure [41] and consider escalating respiratory support to NIV or tracheal intubation. Therefore, it is vital that the latter must be readily available and continuous monitoring provided [55].
5. HHHFNCT in the pediatric emergency department

HHHFNCT use has been reported in a number of respiratory conditions seen in the pediatric ED, most commonly bronchiolitis [56]. A retrospective study of 848 patients with any acute respiratory insufficiency severe enough to require ICU admission, including asthma, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and croup, showed 83% reduction in the odds of intubation in the pediatric ED with the implementation of an institution-wide guideline on pediatric HHHFNCT use compared with patients admitted before the availability of HHHFNCT (odds ratio, 0.17; 95% CI 0.06 -0.50; p = 0.001) [57]. Importantly, there was no change in mortality or median ICU length of stay with this implementation. However, the respiratory support used prior to HHHFNCT introduction was not clearly stated, making it difficult to draw definite conclusions from the study. Infants with moderate to severe bronchiolitis started on HHHFNCT in ED have shown a greater improvement in respiratory effort and ability to feed, when compared with standard oxygen therapy [58]. An early pilot ED study in 61 infants aged <12 months with bronchiolitis demonstrated that those managed with HHHFNCT were four times less likely to require ICU admission compared to the standard oxygen therapy group (OR 4.086, 95% CI 1.0 -8.2; p = 0.043) [59]. In a recent multicenter RCT involving 1472 infants with bronchiolitis who presented to the emergency department and general pediatric wards, 12% of those who received HHHFNCT early required escalation of care compared to 23% of those who received standard oxygen therapy (risk difference, -11% points; 95% CI, -15 to -7; p < 0.001). In the latter group, 61% responded to HHHFNCT rescue therapy. There were no significant differences in the duration of oxygen treatment or overall hospital stay. The authors concluded that early institution of HHHFNCT in patients with bronchiolitis is beneficial [18].

Aside from bronchiolitis, NIV options have also been compared in children with pneumonia. Due to the limited ED literature on the use of HHHFNCT in children with pneumonia, we described the results of an open randomized controlled trial in the ICU comparing bubble CPAP, HHHFNCT, and standard oxygen therapy among 225 children in Bangladesh with severe pneumonia. Results showed that while the bubble CPAP group had significantly fewer treatment failures (clinical failure, intubation, deaths) than the standard oxygen therapy group [relative risk (RR) 0.27, 99.7% CI 0.07 -0.99; p = 0.003], there were no significant difference in treatment failures between the bubble CPAP and HHHFNCT groups (RR 0.50, 99.7% 0.11 -2.29; p = 0.175) [60].

Responders to HHHFNCT should demonstrate a decreased respiratory rate, lesser use of accessory muscles, reduced FiO2 requirements, and improved radiological findings [61]. Earlier studies showed the need to escalate from HHHFNCT to higher levels of ventilatory support ranged between 13% and 39% [56,60]. In a retrospective cohort study of HHHFNCT use among children younger than 2 years old, the majority of those with bronchiolitis, pneumonia or asthma who failed HHHFNCT therapy had triage respiratory rate > 90th centile, initial venous pCO2 > 50mmHg and an initial pH < 7.30. However, a diagnosis of bronchiolitis was shown to be protective against the subsequent need for intubation [62].

In a recent prospective pilot study involving 62 children with moderate to severe exacerbation of asthma presenting to ED, those who received HHHFNCT had a significant reduction in respiratory distress within the first two hours of treatment as measured by the pulmonary score, compared to those who received standard oxygen therapy ( p = 0.01). Importantly, no complications were noted. However, there were no differences in length of stay and requirement for further therapies [63].

In summary, early ED studies among children on HHHFNCT showed an improvement in symptoms and potential in reducing mechanical ventilation and ICU admissions, particularly among infants with bronchiolitis which was affirmed in the recent RCT [18].
6. Conclusion

HHHFNCT appears to be an increasingly useful tool in the ED physician ' s armamentarium when faced with a patient in respiratory distress. While promising, prudent patient selection remains key. Future research should focus on specific respiratory pathologies in both adults and children. In the situation of lack of trials on the relevant patient population, care should be taken when extrapolating HHHFNCT use in the ED.
7. Expert commentary

HHHFNCT has emerged as a popular mode of non-invasive respiratory support in recent years. It has been found to be more tolerable and comfortable for patients to converse and express themselves (Level of Evidence 2b). Due to the heated and humidified nature of the gas provided, mouth dryness is reduced, and bronchoconstriction from cold gas is minimized (Level of Evidence 3b). Apart from that, the contact of the nasal cannula is mainly within the nostrils and the cheeks, hence reducing the risk of skin lesions in the other parts of the face as compared to the interfaces used with other current modes of NIV. HHHFNCT setup and application seems to be more straightforward and requires minimal technical skills. Moreover, training can be provided within a short period of time for those who are less familiar with it (Level of Evidence3b).

However, one of the drawbacks of using HHHFNCT is the certain degree of experience that is needed to decide which acutely ill adult or child would benefit from this form of noninvasive respiratory support over other modes. This is particularly important to minimize the delay in utilizing the best tool to support a patient with respiratory distress. Like with any mode of treatment, having made the decision to administer HHHFNCT, it is crucial to assess the patient ' s response to the intervention. Constant monitoring is required to prompt the clinician to escalate therapy if necessary. Given the nature of ED and its high turnover of patients, this may prove to be the most challenging obstacle to the use of HHHFNCT, where the staff to patient ratio is low. Adequately trained health professionals within this clinical setting has to be available before HHHFNCT can be used routinely in the ED setting. Studies have suggested that HHHFNCT failure may happen within 7 -14 hours, compared to two hours in those using other modes of NIV, in children less than 2 years old, highlighting the need for continual monitoring beyond the ED [37]. Similarly, in adults, there have been concerns raised about the potential delay in escalation of treatment when on HHHFNCT, leading to worsening clinical outcome [64] (Level of Evidence 2b).

Although HHHFNCT has been used extensively for many years in the neonatal population, its use in infants and older children is still somewhat limited. Current indications are unclear, but is thought to be similar to other modes of NIV [62]. There are reports of success in bronchiolitis, pneumonia, asthma, recurrent apneas, neuromuscular diseases, and heart failure. Overall, the evidence is either conflicting or lacking, particularly in the context of initializing HHHFNCT in ED. Until then, extrapolation of data from pediatric intensive care studies may be necessary. From recent studies in bronchiolitis (Level of Evidence 1b) and asthma (Level of Evidence 3b), early use of HHHFNCT seems to be beneficial compared to standard oxygen therapy [18,63]. The next steps may be to compare early use of HHHFNCT with that of CPAP in ED. In the meantime, a multicenter RCT feasibility trial named FIRST ABC is being conducted to compare the use of HHHFNCT and CPAP as first-line non-invasive mode of ventilatory support within the PICU setting [65]. The use of HHHFNCT in other conditions also needs to be addressed to determine which groups of patients would benefit most from it.

Despite the existence of multiple local guidelines, the evidence on recommended starting flow rate, when and how to wean, remains unclear. Part of the reason is the difficulty and impracticality of measuring the amount of positive pressure generated within the airway. It would be ideal to be able to detect these pressures using a sensor integrated within the HHHFNCT circuit. With this knowledge, flow rates can be adjusted accordingly to maximize its use and minimize complications. Although this may be difficult to achieve due to the nature of an open circuit with mouth opening, perhaps integration and averages of transient readings obtained may be feasible.

Similarly, adult studies on HHHFNCT have mainly involved small number of patients. These studies have demonstrated that HHHFNCT can be utilized in a wide range of respiratory illnesses and reduces patients ' work of breathing. However, its clinical efficacy remains uncertain, with no significant difference in escalation to mechanical ventilation, length of stay in ED or rate of mortality, when compared to conventional treatment. It is important to bear in mind that the population in ED is heterogeneous resulting in a dilution of true effect in specific respiratory conditions.

Given the scarcity of evidence available, HHHFNCT should be used with caution in infants and children, particularly outside the PICU setting, and also in adults. As with all treatment, a critical approach has to be taken once HHHFNCT is initiated, to look for improvement in clinical signs and symptoms, and monitoring for potential deterioration that requires escalation of intervention.

In terms of cost-effectiveness of HHHFNCT compared to standard oxygen therapy or NIV, computer-based models from the United Kingdom have demonstrated that when HHHFNCT is used as first-line treatment, HHHFNCT is estimated to save £469 (USD $608) per patient compared to standard oxygen therapy and £611 (USD$793) per patient compared to NIV [66]. In another study carried out in Finland comparing HHHFNCT and standard oxygen therapy in infants with bronchiolitis, investigators found that the treatment cost of each episode was between € 1,312 -2,644 (USD $1,786 -3,600) in the HHHFNCT group compared to € 1,598 -3,764 (USD$2,175 -5,125) in the standard oxygen therapy group. They also found that the intensive care unit admission rates were lower for the HHHFNCT group than for the standard oxygen therapy group [67].
8. Five-year view

Based on the ease of administration, coupled to the potential benefits including patient satisfaction, we expect that the use of HHHFNCT will increase in the future overall despite the lack of full understanding of the mechanism of action and pressures provided. We foresee that there would be an increasing number of ED health professionals and institutions that will be comfortable initiating HHHFNCT therapy early on in the disease process as more training is provided in this field. There will probably be more studies tailored towards specific conditions, and comparison between HHHFNCT and standard oxygen therapy or HHHFNCT versus CPAP, as we have noted in the past few years. Similarly, evidence on starting flow rates would become more available, particularly whether using higher flow rates than currently recommended for a given duration would be advantageous, bearing in mind the potential complications that may be associated with this. From the device point of view, a form of non-invasive pressure sensor within the circuit interface would represent a medical advancement as this can provide more information for the clinicians, especially during the weaning phase.
Key issues

The mechanism of action of HHHFNCT includes nasopharyngeal dead space ' wash-out ' , increase in the capacity for oxygen delivery, the generation of positive end expiratory pressure and improvement in respiratory mechanics.
HHHFNCT is more tolerable for patients and easier for clinical staff to administer compared to other methods of non-invasive respiratory support.

Use of HHHFNCT has extended beyond intensive care practice to ED, and found to be safe, with the ability to reduce work of breathing of patients in acute respiratory and cardiac illnesses. It is also better tolerated.
Studies in pediatric HHHFNCT use in the ED setting is limited, but early use showed clinical improvement in those with bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and asthma.

Pathophysiologie des akuten Atemversagens im Kindesalter

Das respiratorische Versagen ist die häufigste Indikation für eine nichtelektive Aufnahme auf die pädiatrische Intensivstation [17, 29]. Die obstruktive Bronchitis und die Bronchiolitis des sehr kleinen Säuglings im Rahmen viraler Atemwegsinfektionen stellen sich in großen Erhebungen als die häufigste Ursache für ein Atemversagen dar [17]. Oft kann das 'respiratory syncytial virus' (RSV) nachgewiesen werden. Aufgrund direkt zytopathischer Effekte am Bronchialepithel kommt es bei einer RSV-Infektion zu Epithelzellnekrosen,Inflammationsowie Detritus und Mukusansammlung in den mittlerenundsehrkleinenAtemwegemit konsekutiver Erhöhung des Atemwegswiderstandes [52, 55]. Durch einen Anstieg des exspiratorischen Lungenvolumens mit Überblähung der Lunge durch die eingeschränkte Exspiration kommtes zur Verschiebung der Atemmittellage in einen unphysiologischen Bereich, sodass zur Aufrechterhaltung eines ausreichenden Atemzeitvolumens eine hohe Atemarbeit geleistet werden muss [30, 57]. Die Dekompensation der Atempumpe zeigt sich an einer progredienten Hyperkapnie bei klinischen Erschöpfungszeichen des tachypnoischen Säuglings oder Kindes [6, 57].
Akutes Asthma bei älteren Kindern stellt sich in der klinischen Symptomatik vergleichbar der obstruktiven Bronchitis des kleinen Kindes dar. Auch hier kommt es zu einer Einengung der kleinen Atem-

Nichtinvasive Beatmung bei Kindern mit akuter respiratorischer Insuffizienz

wege und zu einer Mukusansammlung. ImGegensatzzumkleinenKindstehthier jedoch neben der Dyskrinie die Schwellung und Konstriktion der bronchialen Muskelschichten im Vordergrund, was dieteilweiseReversibilitätderAtemwegswiderstandserhöhung durch Betamimetika und antiinflammatorische Medikamente erklärt [10].

Seltener führt die Obstruktion im Bereich des Larynx oder der großen Atemwege bei Pseudokrupp, Epiglottitis, bakterieller Tracheitis oder durch einen Fremdkörper zum Atemversagen [17]. Auch hier kommt es final zum Versagen der Atempumpe mit vorwiegend ventilatorischer Insuffizienz bei weitgehend nicht gestörtem alveolärem Gasaustausch, bedingt durch den erhöhten Atemwegswiderstand.
» Bei alveolären Erkrankungen steht die Hypoxie im Vordergrund

Akute Störungen des alveolären Gasaustausches, wie z. B. durch eine ambulant erworbene Pneumonie oder durch ein 'acute respiratory distress syndrom' (ARDS), führen vorwiegend zum hypoxämischen Atemversagen. Bakterielle oder virale Erreger induzieren die Freisetzung von Zytokinen durch Alveolarmakrophagen, das Einwandern von Granulozyten und anderen proinflammatorischen Zellen. Die folgende Kaskade von Inflammation hat zum Ziel, pathogene Erreger zu eliminieren, bewirkt aber auch eine Sekretion von Proteinen in das Alveolarlumen, eine intraalveoläre Ödembildung, den Verbrauch von Surfactant und in der Folge auch ein interstitielles Ödem. Die resultierende Verschlechterung der Diffusionskapazität an der alveolär-kapillären Grenzfläche führt zur Gasaustauschstörung. Aufgrund der im Vergleich zur CO2-Diffusion schlechteren Diffusion von Sauerstoff und des größeren Effektes intrapulmonaler Shunts auf den Sauerstoffpartialdruck steht die Hypoxie bei den alveolären Erkrankungen im Vordergrund [9].

Schwerere Pneumonien mit beatmungspflichtigem Atemversagen sind eher seltener bei ansonsten gesunden Kindern, gefährdeter hingegen sind Kinder mit chronischen Erkrankungen ('acute on chronic'; [17, 62]). Risikofaktoren sind klassisch neuromuskuläre Erkrankungen mit Atemmuskelund Hustenschwäche, geistige Behinderung und Zerebralparesen. Primär pulmonale Grunderkrankungen wie zystische Fibrose und primäre ziliäre Dyskinesie sowie auch Immundefekte prädisponieren ebenfalls für ein schweres Atemversagen.
Physiologische Effekte nichtinvasiver Beatmung

Nichtinvasive Beatmung (NIV) beschreibt die Beatmung mit einer getriggerten oder nichtgetriggerten Erhöhung des Beatmungsdrucks während der Inspiration (positiver inspiratorischer Druck, PIP) und einem niedrigen Druckniveau während der Exspiration

[DOCLING_PAGE 2]
Leitthema

Abb. 1 8 Nichtinvasive Beatmung mit einer Full-face-Maske.5JahrealtePatientinmitdystonerspastischerZerebralparesenachKernikterus undakutemAtemversagenbeiBronchopneumonie. (APCV ['assisted, pressure controlled ventilation'] -Modus, PIP [positiver inspiratorischer Druck]/PEEP [positiver endexspiratorischer Druck] 23/10 cm H2O, Ti 1,0 s. f = 26/min)

(positiver endexspiratorischer Druck, PEEP). Durch NIV kann bereits im Säuglings- und Kindesalter Atemarbeit wirksam reduziert werden [14, 45]. DadurchwirddieAtemmuskulaturentlastet [6, 45] und kann sich regenerieren [8, 59]. Das Tidalvolumen wird durch den positiven inspiratorischen Druck vergrößert, was einen CO2-Abfall und eine Reduktion der Atemfrequenz aufgrund der verbesserten Ventilation zur Folge hat [14, 61].
» Hypoxämisches Atemversagen ist nur bedingt einer NIVTherapie zugänglich

Kontinuierlicher positiver Atemwegsdruck (CPAP) beschreibt die Atemunterstützung mit einem gleichförmig erhöhten Atemwegsdruck über die Inspiration und die Exspiration ohne Veränderung des Druckniveaus. Durch CPAP bzw. den PEEP während der NIV wird der obere Atemweg offengehalten, was durch die Reduktion des Atemwegswiderstandes zusätzlich die Atemarbeit reduziert [55]. CPAP/PEEP schient möglicherweise ebenfalls die mittleren und kleinen Atemwege während der Exspiration in geringem Maße [55]. Wahrscheinlich wird Atelektasenbildung durch PEEP reduziert [35], die Daten sind aber weniger eindeutig [55].
Abb. 2 8 NasaleProngsbeimSäugling.4MonatealterSäuglingmitviralemInfektundschwerer Tracheomalazie (CPAP [kontinuierlicher positiver Atemwegsdruck] max. 12cm H2O)

In begrenztem Umfang kann auch der Gasaustausch über die Erhöhung des mittleren Atemwegsdrucks positiv beeinflusst werden. Aufgrund der intermittierend hohen Leckagen, wie auch durch gelegentlich notwendiges Absetzen der Beatmungsmaske, kommt es jedoch immer wieder kurzzeitig zu einem Druckabfall. Wenige Millisekunden eines Druckabfalls können bei stark eingeschränkter Compliance zum Alveolarkollaps und damit zur Hypoxie führen [47, 51]. Dies erklärt, warum das hypoxämische Atemversagen, im Gegensatz zum hyperkapnischen Versagen der Atempumpe, nur sehr bedingt einer Therapie durch NIV zugänglich ist [43, 61].
Interface und Technik

Erst seit wenigen Jahren steht ein größeres Sortiment an konfektionierten Masken für Säuglinge und Kinder zur Verfügung, was die Anwendung der NIV bei akutem Atemversagen deutlich vereinfacht hat. Bei leichtem hyperkapnischem Atemversagen, wie z. B. bei einem Patienten mit neuromuskulärer Grunderkrankung und Virusinfekt, ist eine nasale Maske ausreichend. Schweres Atemversagen und zusätzliche Hypoxie erfordern Full-face-Masken, welche aufgrund der viel niedrigeren Leckagen einen höheren Spitzendruck und PEEP erlauben ( . Abb. 1 ).

Bei jungen Säuglingen kommen außerdem sog. 'Prong'-Systeme als nasale Interfaces zum Einsatz. Diese sind Weiterentwicklungen aus der Neonatologie. Ihr Vorteil ist ein relativ fester Sitz, trotz wenig beeinträchtigender Befestigung. Entsprechend gut ist oft die Toleranz. Bei denoftgroßenLeckagenbeiVerwendung von Prongs ist ein Triggern der Beatmung für den Patienten manchmal nicht möglich. Die Einstellung von Backupfrequenzen, welche geringfügig über der Spontanatemfrequenz liegen, erlaubt oft eine Synchronisierung der Beatmungshübe mit den Spontanatemzügen. Bei hohen Leckagen kann jedoch das exspiratorische Tidalvolumen nicht mehr zuverlässig gemessen werden ( . Abb. 2 ).

Bei geringer Masken-Compliance bei Säuglingen und Kleinkindern ist auch ein relativ groß zu wählender mononasaler pharyngealer Tubus immer noch ein mögliches Interface [60]. Man verwendet hierfür am besten weiche nichtblockbare Tuben. Topisches Lokalanästhetikum erleichtert dem Patienten die Anlage. Ein Pharyngealtubus verhindert auch das Zurückfallen der Zunge, was in vielen Situationen und besonders bei Kindern mit Zerebralparese die Atemmechanik verbessert.

EinenichtinvasiveBeatmungvonKindernmitBeatmungshelmwirdvonitalienischen Arbeitsgruppen beschrieben [7, 28] und war in Studien bei Erwachsenen sogar vorteilhaft [49]. Die Verwendung eines Beatmungshelms ist im deutschsprachigen Raum jedoch die Ausnahme.

Prinzipiell erlauben die meisten Intensivrespiratoren auch die Anwendung der NIV im Kindesalter. Die begrenzten Flowraten, die einige Geräte liefern, die auf Druckluft und Drucksauerstoff angewiesen sind (z. B. 6-30 l/min, Evita 4, Pädiatriemodus), ermöglichen nicht die EffizienzmodernererTurbinengeräte,die wesentlichhöhereFlowratenliefern(z. B. 0-240 l/min, V60, Phillips Respironics). HoheFlowratensindvorteilhaft,umtrotz eventuellen Leckagen noch ausreichendenBeatmungsdruckzugenerieren.Moderne Turbinengeräte, die speziell für die NIV entwickelt wurden, sind teilweise auch für Kinder zugelassen und sollten vorzugsweise für die NIV zur Anwendung kommen [54, 61].

Bronchiolitis

Die Wirksamkeit der nichtinvasiven Beatmung zur Behandlung der Brochiolitis bei Säuglingen und Kleinkindern ist durch randomisierte Studien [63], eine Crossoverstudie [58] und mehrere Kohortenstudienbelegt.NIV/CPAPverbessert den Gasaustausch und entlastet von Atemarbeit [45, 55].

Yanez et al. randomisierten 50 Kinder mitAtemversagenzuNIVoderStandardtherapie ohne NIV. Die meisten Säuglinge und Kinder (medianes Alter 18 vs. 16 Monate) litten an viralen Atemwegsinfekten und Bronchiolitis, nur einzelne an Asthma oder Pneumonie. Atemfrequenz und Herzfrequenz nahmen in der NIV-Gruppe signifikant schneller ab als in der Gruppe der Standardtherapie. PaO2/FiO2 verbesserte sich in der NIV-Gruppebereits in der ersten Stunde nachTherapiebeginn. Die Intubationsrate nach standardisierten Intubationskriterien betrug 28 % in der NIV-Gruppe und 60 % in der Standardtherapiegruppe. Beobachtete Nebenwirkungen waren vor allem lokale Hautirritationen durch die Atemmaske [63].

In ca. 80 % der Krankheitsfälle kann selbst bei schwerer Bronchiolitis durch NIV eine Intubation vermieden werden [38]. Die Stabilisierung von Kindern mit Atemversagen bei Bronchiolitis durch NIV oder CPAP ist heutzutage Therapie der Wahl auf pädiatrischen Intensivstationen [15, 24]. Der präklinische Einsatz könnte hier hilfreich sein [13].
Asthma

Kleinere randomisierte Studienmitniedrigen Fallzahlen sowie Kohortenstudien zeigen Behandlungserfolge der NIV bei Kindern und Erwachsenen mit akuter Asthmaexazerbation auf [4, 41, 58]. In den meisten Studien wurde vor allem die Verbesserung physiologischer Parameter gezeigt, für einen echten Vorteil im Langzeitoutcome oder für kurzfristige Parameter wie Intubationsraten sind die Fallzahlen jedoch zu klein bzw. es wurde keine Kontrollgruppe untersucht.
Zusammenfassung · Abstract

Nichtinvasive Beatmung bei Kindern mit akuter respiratorischer Insuffizienz
Zusammenfassung

Akutes Atemversagen kann auch im Kindesalter mit nichtinvasiver Beatmung (NIV) behandelt werden. In den letzten Jahren wurden die technischen Voraussetzungen der NIV-Beatmungsgeräte für das Kindesalter verbessert, zudem steht heutzutage eine größere Auswahl an konfektionierten nasalen und Full-face-Masken für Kinder ab dem Säuglingsalter als Interface zur Verfügung. Vor allem Kinder mit hyperkapnischem Atemversagen profitieren von der NIV. Evidenz für Vorteile der NIV besteht für die Bronchiolitis, Asthma sowie für das 'Acute-on-chronic'-Atemversagen, d. h. ein Atemversagen bedingt durch eine akute Infektion bei einer zugrunde liegenden neuromuskulären Erkrankung, Zerebralparese oder einer chronischen Lungenerkrankung wie der zystischen Fibrose. Nichtinvasive Beatmung ist bei prolongiertem Weaning von invasiver Beatmung und bei Fehlbildungen des oberen Atemwegs hilfreich. Alveoläre Erkrankungen mit vorwiegend hypoxämischem Atemversagen wie ambulant erworbene Pneumonien oder das 'acute respiratory distress syndrome' (ARDS) stellen keine Indikationen für die NIV dar. Aufgrund relevanter möglicher Nebenwirkungen und der Möglichkeit der schnellen Verschlechterung des Gasaustauschs bei NIV-Versagen sollte die NIV auf der pädiatrischen Intensivstation mit der Möglichkeit zu einem raschen Wechsel auf einen invasiven Beatmungszugang stattfinden.
Schlüsselwörter
Beatmungsgeräte · Nebenwirkungen · Acute respiratory distress syndrome · Weaning · High flow nasal cannula
Noninvasive ventilation in pediatric acute respiratory failure
Abstract

Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) may be used to treat pediatric acute respiratory failure. Recent improvements in ventilator technology and availability of nasal and full face masks for infants and children have simplified the use of NIV even in the smallest children. Mainly patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure may benefit from noninvasive ventilation. There is some evidence available that supports the use of NIV in viral bronchiolitis, asthma and acute on chronic respiratory failure in patients with neuromuscular or chronic pulmonary disease. Furthermore, noninvasive ventilation is beneficial during prolonged weaning from invasive ventilation and to treat upper airway

Ein Versuch mit NIV zusätzlich zu der Standardtherapie erscheint aber gerechtfertigt, insbesondere dann, wenn das hyperkapnische Atemversagen im Vordergrund steht. Hoher Sauerstoffbedarf war miteinemScheiternderNIVundIntubationen assoziiert, sodass bei im Vordergrund stehender Hypoxie eine invasive Beatmung nicht verzögert werden darf [41].

obstructions. Children suffering from hypoxic respiratory failure, such as communityacquired pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome do not benefit from NIV. Due to possibly relevant side effects and the possibility of rapid deterioration in gas exchange in failure of NIV, invasive ventilation should be readily available; therefore, treatment with noninvasive ventilation for acute respiratory failure in children should be initiated on the pediatric intensive care ward.
Keywords
Ventilation, mechanical · Side effects · Acute respiratory distress syndrome · Weaning · High flow nasal cannula
Exazerbation neuromuskulärer Erkrankungen und Zerebralparese

Dienichtinvasive BeatmungistinderBehandlung der chronischen und sowie der 'akut auf chronischen' respiratorischen InsuffizienzvonPatientenmitneuromuskulären Erkrankungen sowie bei Thoraxund Wirbelsäulendeformitäten etabliert und indiziert. Sie entlastet die chronisch überlastete Muskulatur, reduziert Dys- und Atelektasen und erhöht das Atemminutenvolumen und die Oxygenierung [50]. Durch die unterstützte Inspiration und das damit einhergehende höhere Atemzugvolumen können die Patienten oft auch besser Sekret abhusten. Bei akutenInfektionenmussderBeatmungsdruck bei einer Vortherapie mit häuslicher Beatmung erheblich erhöht werden. Eine zusätzliche O2-Therapie sollte bei Patienten mit neuromuskulären Erkrankungen so wenig wie möglich verabreicht werden, da die Atelektasenbildung durch zusätzlichen Sauerstoff gefördert wird [11, 37]. Bei hohem Risiko für bakterielle Superinfektionen sollten Patienten mit schwachem Hustenstoß auch bei fieberhaften Virusinfektionen mit Antibiotika behandelt werden [22]. Durch die NIV kann die drohende Intubation häufig noch vermieden werden.

Auch bei Patienten mit Zerebralparesen mit und ohne Skoliosen kann die NIV den Gasaustausch und die Ventilation im Infekt deutlich verbessern. Letztendlich kommen ähnliche Mechanismen wiebeidenklassischenneuromuskulären Erkrankungen zum Tragen, d. h. schwacher Hustenstoß, Sekretretention, niedriges Atemzugvolumen und Atelektasenneigung. Unserer Erfahrung nach sprechen viele Patienten hervorragend auf NIV an.
Exazerbation der zystischen Fibrose

Intubation und invasive Beatmung ist bei akuter Exazerbation der zystischen Fi- brose (CF) mit einer hohen Mortalität und schlechtem Langzeitoutcome assoziiert [12]. Andererseits ist bekannt, dass durch NIV der Gasaustausch bei Patienten mit CF deutlich gebessert werden kann [18]. Ein primärer Behandlungsversuch mit NIV ist von daher bei Patienten mit akuter Atemwegsinfektion und CF gerechtfertigt. Ein Problem stellt nicht selten die Patientencompliance dar. Oft tolerieren Patienten mit CF die Atemmaske schlecht und entscheiden sich trotz möglicher Stabilisierung der physiologischen Parameter gegen die nichtinvasive Atemunterstützung.
Extubationsversagen

Eine nichtinvasive Beatmung hat sich bei Kindern mit hohem Risiko für ein Extubationsversagen bewährt [23, 42]. Als Riskofaktoren sind hier die vorausgehende prolongierte invasive Beatmung, persistierende Gasaustauschstörung bei Extubation, chronische neuromuskuläre Erkrankung oder chronisch parenchymatöse Lungenerkrankung zu nennen. Wichtig ist, dass der Beatmungszugang unmittelbar von invasiv auf nichtinvasiv gewechselt wird und der Patient dann schrittweise von der NIV entwöhnt wird [3, 20, 21]. Dagegen ist die NIV bei bereits eingetretenem Extubationsversagen nicht indiziert [54, 61]. Oft ist eine NIV dann nicht mehr effektiv. Aus Studien an Erwachsenengehtsogarhervor,dasssich die Mortalität erhöhte, wenn bei eingetretenem Extubationsversagen noch ver- sucht wurde, durch Beginn von NIV die Reintubation zu verhindern [16].
Ambulant erworbene Pneumonie und ARDS

Nichtinvasive BeatmungzurBehandlung der ambulant erworbenen Pneumonie unddesARDSbeiKindernohnezusätzlicheGrunderkrankungistwahrscheinlich nicht indiziert [54, 61]. Große randomisierte Studien an Erwachsenen konnten keinen Vorteil in Bezug auf Mortalität oderMorbiditätnachweisen[5,26].Möglicherweise ist es bei diesem vor allem hypoxämischen Atemversagen sicherer, das ateminsuffiziente Kind direkt zu intubieren und invasiv zu beatmen.

Ein großes Risiko bei der Behandlung des hypoxämischen Atemversagens durch NIV ist die sehr akut auftretende Hypoxie,falls es z. B. durch Undichtigkeit der Maske zum Alveolarkollaps kommt. In Teilen kollabierte Lungenareale lassen sich dann nicht immer wieder eröffnen. Die dann notwendige Intubation eventuell aus der Hypoxie heraus kann sehr risikoreich sein und es können Komplikationen bis hin zum Herzstillstand mit Reanimationssituationen auftreten [27].

Aufgrund des höheren Risikos für eine ventilatorassoziierte Pneumonie und Katheterinfektionen wurde der Vorteil einer NIV bei der Gruppe der immunsupprimierten Patienten bisher höher als bei Nichtimmunsupprimierten eingeschätzt,sodassdiesePatientengruppe eine Sonderstellung pro NIV auch bei hypoxämischemAtemversagenzuhaben schien [1, 33]. In neueren Studien konnte aber auch hier kein Vorteil mehr nachgewiesen werden, sodass bei hypoxischem Atemversagen und Immunsuppression nach Standardtherapie und ggf. 'high flow' nasalem Sauerstoff die Intubation bei einer Verschlechterung zeitnah vorgenommen werden sollte [39, 40].
Nebenwirkungen und Kontraindikationen
KontraindikationenfürnichtinvasiveBeatmung sind in . Tab. 1 aufgeführt [19, 61].

Die häufigste Nebenwirkung der NIV sind von der Maske verursachte Druck- stellen bis hin zu tiefen Ulzera. Diese treten vor allem dann auf, wenn die NIV ohne längere Pausen angewendet werden muss. Heutzutage sind Druckstellen durch den Einsatz der weicheren neueren Masken deutlich seltener geworden. Es lohnt sich meist nicht, durch zu festes Anziehen der Maskenbefestigung alle Leckagen zu beseitigen, dafür aber Druckstellen zu provozieren. Ein maßvolles AnziehenderGurtemitAkzeptanz geringer Leckagen ist langfristig oft vorteilhafter [61].

Bei einem hohen Beatmungsdruck kommt es gelegentlich zu erheblicher Aerophagie und Magendistension, was wiederum die Atemmechnik beeinträchtigen kann. Hier wird eventuell das Ableiten der Luft durch eine Magensonde notwendig. Eine PEG (perkutane endoskopische Gastrostomie) -Sonde sollte zur Entlüftung des Magens offen gelassen werden.

Selten können, insbesondere bei starker Dyspnoe, ein Pneumothorax oder Mediastinalemphysem auftreten. Gerade bei einem hohen Beatmungsdruck und beiVerschlechterungdesGasaustausches sollte deshalb großzügig eine radiologische Verlaufskontrolle erfolgen [27, 43].
» Eine Verschlechterung der Beatmungssituation muss frühzeitig erkannt werden

Die Hauptgefahr der NIV besteht darin, dass eine progrediente Verschlechterung des Gasaustausches zu spät erkannt wird und das Risiko für Komplikationen bei der dann notwendigen Intubation stark ansteigt. Wenn der Patient auch unter NIV mit hohen Drücken bei Spontanatmungnichtmehrausreichendoxygeniert und ventiliert, ist es eher unwahrscheinlich, dass man dies dann in der Intubationssituation mit Maske und Beatmungsbeutel erreicht. Es ist also unbedingt notwendig, eine Verschlechterung der Beatmungssituation an der NIV frühzeitig wahrzunehmen und den Beatmungszugang von nichtinvasiv auf invasiv mit entsprechenden Sicherheitsmargen vorzunehmen [27].

Aus diesen Gründen sollte die NIV bei akuter respiratorischer Insuffizienz nur dann erfolgen, wenn eine Möglichkeit zur invasiven Beatmung besteht, wie es auf der pädiatrischen Intensivstation der Fall ist. Ein Monitoring während der NIV sollte Pulsoxymetrie, Herzfrequenz, Atemfrequenz, regelmäßige Blutgase, ggf. besser durch arteriellen Zugang undFiO2,umfassen.Verschlechterungen des Gasaustausches und Erschöpfungszeichen des Kindes müssen wahrgenommen und ggf. durch einen Wechsel auf eineinvasiveBeatmungbeantwortetwerden ( . Möglicherweise entstehen weitere Vorteile der HFNC durch das Auswaschen von CO2 aus dem Nasopharynx und eine damit verbundene funktionelle Totraumverkleinerung [46]. Ein weiterer VorteilistdieVerwendungeinesbefeuchteten Atemgases, was bei der Sekretolyse hilft und ggf. auch Atemwegswiderstände reduziert [25]. Der Hauptvorteil der HFNC gegenüber der NIV ist die deutlich bessere Toleranz [56] und die fast fehlenden Nebenwirkungen, weshalb die HFNC bereits häufig in Notaufnahmen, peripheren Stationen und pädiatrischen Intensivstationen eingesetzt wird [53].

In klinischen Untersuchungen zeigt die HFNC einen leichten Vorteil gegenüberderStandardtherapiemitLow-flowSauerstoff[26,44].InmehrerenKohorten wurde mit Einführung der HFNC und imVergleich mit historischen Kontrollen vor Einführung der HFNC-Therapie eine erheblichReduktionanIntubationenvon KindernmitAtemversagen(vorallembei Bronchiolitis) beobachtet. Die Dauer der Bronchiolitis und das Langzeitoutcome kann jedoch durch die HFNC nicht beeinflusst werden.

Die klassische NIV über eine Maske ist der HFNC aber in Bezug auf Effektivität überlegen. In der TRAMONTANEStudie wurden 142 Säuglinge mit mittelschwerer und schwerer Bronchiolitis zu HFNC oder nCPAP randomisiert [44]. Ein Therapieversagen wurde in 51 % unter HFNC und 31% unter NIV beobachtet. Auch in Studien bei Erwachsenen konnten positive Effekte der HFNC nach Extubation [31, 32] und beim akuten Atemversagen [26, 36] nachgewiesen werden.AuchbeiKindernsolltedieRolle der HFNC bei hypoxischem Atemversagen in Zukunft in Studien noch besser charakterisiert werden. Bei hyperkapnischem Atemversagen erscheint die NIV effektiver. Bei der hervorragenden Toleranz der HFNC ist ein stufenweises Vorgehen mit anfänglich HFNC und einem Wechsel auf NIV bei einer Verschlechterung gerechtfertigt.
