4 Nichtinvasive Beatmung hat einen hohen Stellenwert bei der Behandlung von Säuglingen und Kindern mit akutem Atemversagen. Vor allem das hyperkapnische Atemversagen lässt sich gut mit NIV behandeln.

REVIEW
High flow nasal cannula in the pediatric intensive care unit
Jason A. Clayton a , Katherine N. Slain a , Steven L. Shein a and Ira M. Cheifetz b

a Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine, Rainbow Babies & Children's Hospital, Cleveland, Ohio USA; b Division of Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Medicine, Rainbow Babies & Children's Hospital, Cleveland, Ohio USA
ABSTRACT

Introduction: The use of high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) has become widely used in pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) throughout the world. The rapid adoption has outpaced the number of studies evaluating the safety and efficacy in a variety of pediatric diseases/conditions.

Areas covered: This scoping review begins with the definition and mechanisms of action of HFNC and then follows with a review of the literature focused on studies performed on critically ill children cared for in the PICU. The PubMed database was searched with a pediatric filter from the time period 2000 to 2021.

Expert opinion: The rapid adoption of HFNC in PICUs has largely been driven by changes in institu­ tional practices and small observational studies. There is a lack of adequately powered studies evaluat­ ing patient-centered outcomes, such as intubation rates, mortality, PICU, and hospital length of stay. Given the wide variability in flow rates and clinical indications, more research is needed to better define effective flow rates for different disease states as well as markers of treatment success and failure. One particular entity that is poorly studied is the use of HFNC in those at risk for developing pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS).
1. Introduction

The use of high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) has become widely used in intensive care units (ICUs) throughout the world. First described in the early 1990s, its use was pioneered as an alternative to noninvasive positive pressure for the treatment of respiratory dis­ tress syndrome in neonates, including premature infants [1-5]. In parallel, the use of HFNC was studied in adult populations with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [6,7], hypoxemic respira­ tory failure [8-11], and post-extubation respiratory distress [12-15]. Application of HFNC in pediatric patients was initially slow to be adopted, but subsequently, its use and study has increased sig­ nificantly. A PubMed search for 'high flow nasal cannula' with a pediatric search filter shows an exponential increase in manu­ scripts from a single study in 2001 to over 100 in 2019.

While initially studied in children with acute viral bronch­ iolitis, disease indications for treatment with HFNC have broa­ dened to include asthma, acute hypoxemic respiratory failure including pneumonia, obstructive sleep apnea, and postextubation respiratory distress. The purpose of this scoping review is to provide an overview of the literature as it relates to the use of HFNC in the PICU. After a brief description of the currently accepted mechanisms of gas exchange during HFNC, we will describe the available literature regarding its use in the pediatric critical care environment.
1.1. Methodology
We performed a scoping review by searching PubMed using the key phrase 'high flow nasal cannula' with a pediatric filter

within the time period of 2000 through 2021. Abstracts and reference lists were individually examined by one author (JC) to retrieve articles that studied HFNC specific to the PICU setting. Only articles written in English were considered. Both observational studies and prospective trials were included in this review.
2. Definition and mechanisms of action

HFNC is sometimes referred to as heated, humidified, highflow nasal cannula, highlighting all the important aspects that define its use. Traditionally, unconditioned flow rates of less than 1-2 L/min in neonates and less than 4-6 L/min in chil­ dren are classified as low-flow, or conventional, nasal cannula [16]. While there is no established flow rate that defines high flow, many studies have postulated that flow delivery should meet or exceed the patient's peak spontaneous inspiratory flow [17-23]. As HFNC has become more commonly used, researchers have determined that flow rates of 1-2 L/kg/min can be effective in treating children with respiratory distress [17-23].

Several mechanisms may explain the beneficial effects of HFNC; however, the relative effective contribution of each mechanism in an individual patient is generally not entirely clear. As one of the primary functions of the nasopharynx is to warm and humidify the air that we breathe, the first mechan­ ism by which HFNC is effective is by augmenting the delivery of warm, humidified gas via a HFNC system. HFNC maintains the hydration status of the nasal mucosa, reduces the

Article highlights

Several mechanisms are postulated to demonstrate efficacy of HFNC, including improving mucociliary clearance and reducing bronchoreac­ tivity with heated and humidified gas, increasing effective FiO 2 by providing oxygen-rich gas, washing out nasopharyngeal deadspace, improving work of breathing by improving diaphragm dynamics, and reducing airway resistance by applying positive pharyngeal pressure.

The application of HFNC in the pediatric intensive care unit, initially studied as an alternative for noninvasive ventilation, has largely been driven by small observational studies that have been generally con­ sistent in showing a therapeutic benefit with respect to vital signs and clinical measures of the patient's work of breathing, although defini­ tive outcome data are lacking.
The most common and well-studied indication for HFNC in the PICU is acute bronchiolitis.
For asthma, aerosol delivery via HFNC is significantly reduced with higher flow rates and smaller cannula sizes.
More research is needed in patients at risk for PARDS, including optimal flow rates, risk factors for progression to PARDS, and factors related to prevention of progression to PARDS.

There is wide variability in practice with respect to flow settings and disease indications as well as a lack of studies evaluating indications for initiating, escalating, and weaning of HFNC therapy.
When compared to conventional therapies, HFNC appears safe in a variety of conditions including asthma, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and post-extubation respiratory distress.

Given the broad acceptance of HFNC and perceived lack of equipoise, future studies utilizing the tools of Quality Improvement may be helpful to design initiation and weaning protocols and appropriate flow rates for a range of disease indications.

metabolic work required to condition dry, cold gas, improves mucociliary clearance, decreases airway resistance, and reduces insensible water losses [16,21,23]. Also, by not desic­ cating the nasal passages, HFNC provides more comfort and better tolerance of the higher flow rates of gas [16,21,23,24].

A second mechanism proposes that HFNC significantly reduces the entrainment of ambient air, thereby increasing the effective fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2 ), contrary to low-flow oxygen delivery systems. Third, HFNC is postulated to flush the carbon dioxide-rich gas from the nasopharynx and replace it with oxygen-enriched gas from the HFNC system. This reduces the carbon dioxide that is rebreathed, thus facil­ itating improved minute ventilation participating in gas exchange. By improving carbon dioxide clearance, work of breathing may also be reduced [25,26]. Fourth, work of breath­ ing is improved by decreasing the pressure × rate product, which is a validated measure of work of breathing [26-29]. Fifth, the application of high-flow gas reduces airway resis­ tance during inspiration [16,21,24,30]. Experimental placement of pharyngeal pressure transducers has demonstrated that distending pressures of up to 6-8 cm H2O can be obtained with flow rates up to 2 L/kg/min [21,23,28,31]. This may effec­ tively stent the soft palate and pharyngeal structures. Overall, careful titration of flow rate contributes to several important characteristics toward making HFNC effective.

Additionally, while HFNC may provide positive distending pressures to the upper airway, the delivery of positive pressure to the distal airways and alveoli remains controversial. Several studies have explored this by measuring pharyngeal pressures as a surrogate for end-expiratory pressure and found that higher flow rates are proportional to higher pharyngeal pres­ sures [21,23,24,28,32]. This is confounded by the open system of HFNC and the intentional use of non-occlusive nasal can­ nula. Therefore, it is unlikely that the alveoli experience similar pressures as seen in the pharynx. Also, in periods of respiratory distress, one may see significant mouth breathing, which further adds to the anatomic leak and loss of distal pressure transduction [33]. Studies have measured esophageal pres­ sures as a marker of intrathoracic pressures during the appli­ cation of HFNC [26,29,31]. In these investigations, the application of HFNC did not demonstrate a significant increase in pressure when compared to low-flow oxygen delivered by nasal cannula.
3. Applications in the pediatric ICU
3.1. Bronchiolitis

By far, the most studied indication for the use of HFNC in the pediatric population has been in infants with bronchiolitis. This is largely due to viral bronchiolitis being a major indica­ tion for pediatric admissions with up to 25% of patients requiring admission to the PICU [34,35].

A single-center retrospective study found that the use of HFNC in infants with bronchiolitis increased from 13% to 66% over a 5-year study period. During that same period, the rate of intubation for this population decreased from 37% to 7% [36]. One-quarter of infants who received HFNC required esca­ lation to a noninvasive ventilation modality. These HFNC nonresponders failed to show improvement in heart rate and respiratory rate, while HFNC responders demonstrated a 20% reduction in heart rate and respiratory rate within 90 minutes of the start of therapy [36]. Similarly, in a separate retrospec­ tive study, McKiernan and colleagues showed that after the introduction of HFNC to their PICU, there was a reduction in rates of intubation and PICU length of stay [37]. Before the introduction of HFNC, the predominant support modality was simple nasal cannula.

Metge and colleagues performed a retrospective study of infants with bronchiolitis during two consecutive seasons of bronchiolitis [38]. During the first season, the primary mode of respiratory support was continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). HFNC was used during the second season. While both modalities showed improvements in heart rate and respiratory rate over time, there were no differences observed when comparing the two modalities over the two seasons. In addi­ tion, the PICU length of stay was not different. There was no comparator group during each season (i.e. standard of care or low flow nasal cannula); so, while HFNC seemed similar to CPAP in terms of patient outcomes, the overall clinical signifi­ cance is difficult to interpret.

In a large, multi-center retrospective database study, Clayton and colleagues evaluated the use of noninvasive ven­ tilation compared to HFNC in infants with acute bronchiolitis [39]. Compared with noninvasive ventilation, initial use with HFNC was associated with a reduced need for intubation (11.0% vs. 20.1%), reduced PICU length of stay (2.8 days vs. 3.7 days), and reduced mortality (0.2% vs. 1.1%). Infants who received HFNC and then subsequently required noninvasive ventilation had similar rates of intubation compared to patients initially receiving noninvasive positive pressure venti­ lation. This retrospective database study was not able to determine risk factors of HFNC failure [39].

In a prospective interventional trial, Ergul and colleagues randomized 60 infants with moderate-to-severe bronchiolitis into groups receiving oxygen via Oxymask or at least 1 L/kg/ min HFNC [40]. The primary outcome was treatment failure, which was defined as the need for escalation of care. There were no treatment failures in the HFNC group, whereas 23% of infants were deemed treatment failures in the Oxymask group. In addition, PICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, and time to weaning from supplemental oxygen were all signifi­ cantly shorter in patients randomized to receive HFNC. Furthermore, improvements in respiratory rate and heart rate were greater in the HFNC group.

In a pilot RCT, Cesar and colleagues randomized 63 infants with bronchiolitis to receive CPAP or HFNC [41]. Treatment failure, defined as the need for escalation of BiPAP or intuba­ tion, was similar in both groups. PICU length of stay was also the same, suggesting equivalence of the two modalities.

In the TRAMONTANE study, Milési and colleagues con­ ducted a multi-center, randomized controlled trial comparing nasal CPAP and HFNC in patients with severe bronchiolitis [42]. The primary outcome was treatment failure, defined as an increase in the modified Woods clinical asthma score, increase in respiratory rate, increase in the EDIN pain/comfort scale [43], and/or more than two episodes of severe apneas. While the HFNC group experienced more treatment failures (50.7% vs. 31.0%), there were no clinical differences in intuba­ tion rates or PICU length of stay compared to nasal CPAP. In addition, total duration of noninvasive respiratory support was not different between the two groups.

In the follow-up TRAMONTANE-2 study, Milési, et al. exam­ ined two flow rates, 2 L/kg/min versus 3 L/kg/min [20]. Treatment failure and intubation rates were the same in both groups (38.7% vs. 38.9%); however, infants treated with 3 L/kg/min were more likely to fail due to patient discomfort and had longer PICU length of stays. Interestingly, the treat­ ment failure rate for the HFNC groups in TRAMONTANE-2 was markedly reduced compared to TRAMONTANE and similar to the CPAP failure rate in the original study. This difference is unlikely to be the result of a change in disease severity but instead is likely secondary to increased clinician expertise with the use of HFNC, gained over the 2 years between study cohorts.

The literature would suggest that the provision of HFNC to infants with viral bronchiolitis is both safe and effective at reducing intubation rates when compared to standard nasal cannula. When compared to noninvasive ventilation modal­ ities, HFNC appears safe, with some studies supporting equiva­ lence to noninvasive ventilation [41,42], whereas others suggest an association with improved outcomes [39]. The rapid acceptance of HFNC may likely be due to the better patient tolerance of this modality when compared to nonin­ vasive positive pressure. In addition, the ease of equipment setup and application of the cannula may make HFNC the preferred respiratory treatment modality in infants with bronchiolitis.
3.2. Asthma

Positive effects of HFNC in critically ill children with asthma who initially present to the emergency department have been reported. In a retrospective study of patients admitted from the pediatric emergency department to the PICU, the intubation rate for pediatric asthma decreased from 5% to 0.6% with the imple­ mentation of a HFNC-use guideline. Despite the decrease in intubation rates, there was no change in PICU length of stay [44]. In a pilot randomized controlled trial of 62 pediatric patients with asthma, those who were randomized to HFNC were more likely to have an improvement in pulmonary score than patients receiving conventional oxygen therapy [45]. Secondary out­ comes did not reveal any differences in PICU length of stay, general ward length of stay, or emergency department dis­ charges. No patients in either group required intubation. However, given the small sample size, conclusions regarding secondary outcomes are likely underpowered.

An observational cohort study of one PICU examined 620 patients who were managed with HFNC during their PICU admission [46]. The most common indication for the use of HFNC was for patients with status asthmaticus at 27% (n = 171), with patients diagnosed with status asthmaticus and pneumonia comprising an additional 14% (n = 85). Few patients in this cohort required escalation to noninvasive ven­ tilation (5.6%) or intubation (4.5%). Of the 171 patients with status asthmaticus treated with HFNC, only 3 (1.7%) required escalation to noninvasive ventilation, and none required intu­ bation. This study also compared a cohort before and after the implementation of HFNC in the PICU and study showed no significant difference in PICU length of stay [46].

A separate retrospective study examined clinical differences in patients with critical asthma treated with HFNC versus noninvasive ventilation [47]. The initial support of noninvasive ventilation or HFNC was decided by the attending PICU phy­ sician and relied 'solely on the physician's self-confidence with the technique.' In the 22 patients who received noninvasive ventilation, none required escalation to intubation and inva­ sive ventilation; whereas 8 of the 20 patients who received HFNC demonstrated failure of treatment and were rescued with noninvasive ventilation, p < 0.001. Despite not finding a difference between the two cohorts with respect to PICU length of stay, when the patients who failed HFNC were examined, it was noted that they had a threefold longer time with ventilator support and double the PICU length of stay when compared to patients receiving noninvasive venti­ lation alone. The application of HFNC in the most severe patients with asthma may delay optimal treatment if failure is not identified and treated early [47].

In a retrospective study from a French PICU, 69 critical asthma patients were included with 39 patients receiving HFNC and 30 patients receiving standard oxygen therapy [48]. The children who received HFNC were sicker as evi­ denced by higher PIM2 score and higher pCO2. These patients had double the length of stay when compared to the cohort of patients only needing conventional oxygen. This difference may be explained in some part by the higher severity of illness, although the authors did not assess this with multi­ variate models [48].

Despite the rapid adoption of HFNC for patients with asthma, current studies do not demonstrate significant improvements in patient outcomes. For patients with more severe disease, HFNC may be a poor choice in that there was a higher incidence of treatment failure requiring rescue with noninvasive ventilation [47]. However, most studies to date are retrospective or observational cohort studies with rela­ tively small sample sizes. Studies are needed to identify risk factors for HFNC failure so that these patients can be more quickly identified, and their therapy intensified.
3.3. Aerosol delivery of medication

It has recently been observed that delivery of aerosolized medications through a HFNC system is variable. In an animal model using scintigraphy to evaluate aerosolized drug deposi­ tion, Réminiac and colleagues demonstrated that a mesh nebulizer placed in a HFNC circuit deposited a similar amount of drug as the standard jet nebulizer and face mask. This was only true at low flow rates of 2 L/min and 4 L/min. At higher flow rates, up to 8 L/min, drug deposition was significantly reduced [49]. Similarly, using a pediatric lung manikin, Moody and colleagues demonstrated that the optimal flow for drug deposition was 3 L/min. For delivery of continuous albuterol, a vibrating mesh nebulizer delivered more drugs than a jet nebulizer [50].

An in vitro study evaluated aerosolized dose delivery using a range of cannula sizes and flow rates. Perry and colleagues demonstrated an inverse relationship between flow rate and nebulized dose delivery. Also, more drugs were delivered with a larger cannula size [51].

The use of the HFNC interface may have important effects on delivering aerosolized medications. In a randomized crossover study comparing standard jet nebulization with a mask to a vibrating mesh nebulizer in-line with HFNC, the authors found improved comfort scores with the use of the mesh nebulizer and HFNC. They postulate this difference was due in part to better tolerance of the cannula versus the face mask as well as fewer disruptions to the patients' sleep or other activities with the integrated mesh nebulizer/HFNC apparatus [52]. This study did not evaluate patient outcomes; so, the overall effectiveness of aerosol delivery with HFNC cannot be determined.

While conditioned gas delivery may lessen the amount of bronchoreactivity in patients with asthma, the poor delivery of nebulized albuterol may negate the theoretical positive effects of HFNC. Manufacturers of HFNC devices are also redesigning delivery devices to improve on aerosolized drug delivery.
3.4. Pneumonia/Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure

A retrospective study conducted over a 3-year period in a PICU showed 40% of patients treated with HFNC as a primary respiratory treatment modality were diagnosed with pneumo­ nia. Overall, in this heterogeneous population, the use of HFNC was associated with improved heart rate, respiratory rate, and SpO2/FiO2 amongst the entire cohort. Predictors of HFNC failure included higher initial FiO2 and lower SpO2/FiO2. The authors did not evaluate separate disease subgroups with respect to changes in SpO2/FiO2 or vital signs, as such it cannot be determined if these population effects are general­ izable to children with pneumonia [53].

In a single-center RCT in India, children and infants admitted with acute respiratory distress were randomized to receive HFNC or conventional oxygen therapy [54]. Pneumonia was the primary diagnosis in 73% of the patients. Treatment failure was defined as not having achieved two or more of the following criteria: respiratory rate reduction by 20%; heart rate reduction by 20%; and FiO2 < 0.5. The odds of treatment failure were 85% lower in patients receiving HFNC compared to those with conventional oxygen therapy. Children with HFNC also had greater improvement in clinical variables, such as respiratory rate and heart rate. Intubation rates, hospital, and ICU length of stay were not examined in this study [54].

In a single-center trial in China, children under 2 years of age with pneumonia were recruited in an emergency ward and randomized to receive HFNC or CPAP [55]. Treatment failure was defined as SpO2 less than 92% and persistent tachycardia and tachypnea after 1 hour of therapy. These patients were subsequently intubated and transferred to a PICU. There was no difference in treatment failure rates between the two groups: HFNC 14% versus CPAP 10%. Hospital length of stay was also similar in both groups. In designing their study, the authors presumed a failure rate of 30% for infants receiving CPAP and 50% for infants on HFNC. This assumption was made based on a study of CPAP versus HFNC in infants with bronchiolitis (TRAMONTANE). Given the large difference in treatment failure rates observed in this study, it is likely that it was underpowered to detect noninferiority as it was originally designed [55].

Chisti and colleagues randomized 225 children with severe pneumonia and hypoxemia to three groups: bubble CPAP, low-flow nasal cannula, and high-flow nasal cannula [56]. Primary outcome was treatment failure defined as two or more of the following: severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 85%) after 30 minutes of study therapy, signs of severe respiratory dis­ tress, and capillary pCO 2 greater than 60 mmHg and pH less than 7.2. There were fewer treatment failures and decreased mortality in the group that received bubble CPAP compared to low-flow nasal cannula. No differences in treatment failure were seen when comparing bubble CPAP to HFNC. The study was stopped prematurely because of the increased mortality in the low-flow oxygen group. It is, therefore, not clear if the absence of differences between CPAP and HFNC is true given the underpowered nature of the study.

Some of the children in the above studies may be categor­ ized as having pediatric ARDS (PARDS), although this informa­ tion was not clearly defined in the above reports. The absence of measurable and consistently applied positive pressure in patients with HFNC precludes its study in patients with PARDS. Recent consensus guidelines from the Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group (PALICC) offered a definition for a group of patients 'at risk' for PARDS that includes those receiving supplemental oxygen via face mask, regular nasal cannula, and HFNC [57]. Future studies are needed in this group of patients on HFNC to define appro­ priate flow-rates, fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2), risk factors for progression of disease, and factors associated with improvement.

This small series of pediatric randomized controlled trials demonstrates that HFNC can improve physiologic variables in children with pneumonia. Outcomes were similar to patients receiving noninvasive positive pressure suggesting therapeu­ tic equivalence. This is supported by the landmark study in critically ill adults by Frat and colleagues. However, while Frat showed a mortality benefit in patients treated with HFNC, this has not been shown in pediatric patients [58]. Larger studies in children are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of HFNC in pediatric pneumonia.
3.5. Post-extubation respiratory distress

Several adult studies have demonstrated reduced reintubation rates when low-risk patients were extubated to HFNC rather than conventional oxygen therapy [13,14] and non-inferiority in high-risk patients extubated to HFNC compared to nonin­ vasive ventilation [12]. A recent meta-analysis confirmed HFNC was non-inferior to noninvasive ventilation in the rate of reintubation and treatment failure [15]. A meta-analysis of preterm newborns showed that extubation to HFNC is not inferior to CPAP [59]. Despite strong evidence in adults and neonates, data in pediatrics are scarce.

A population that is of particular interest are infants who have undergone cardiac surgery. A small physiologic study of 10 infants extubated to HFNC was performed measuring thor­ aco-abdominal synchrony using respiratory inductive plethys­ mography. The authors demonstrated improved thoracoabdominal synchrony with flows of 2 L/kg/min compared to 1 L/kg/min [60]. In another study, pediatric cardiac surgical patients under 18 months of age were randomized to receive HFNC or conventional oxygen after extubation. While the authors did not find any difference in their primary endpoint (pCO2), they were able to demonstrate improvement in PaO2 and PaO2/FiO2 ratio in the patients extubated to HFNC com­ pared to conventional oxygen therapy. The rate of reintuba­ tion, however, did not differ between the two groups [61]. A small prospective observational study examined 20 children who underwent cardiac surgery and were extubated to HFNC. The study showed improvements in respiratory rate but no changes in SpO2, pCO2, heart rate, or lactate. Unfortunately, there was no control group for comparison; so, interpretation of these data is limited [62]. This same group is currently enrolling infants in whom cardiac surgery is planned to eval­ uate for post-extubation pulmonary complications in infants extubated to HFNC [63]. A retrospective study of infants after congenital heart surgery and cardiopulmonary bypass exam­ ined the effect of extubation to HFNC or positive airway pressure. In this propensity-matched analysis, the authors showed that extubation to positive airway pressure was not superior to HFNC with respect to extubation failure. Instead, extubation to positive airway pressures was associated with higher resource utilization and longer lengths of stay [64].

In the general PICU population, an RCT by Akyıldız and colleagues randomized children to extubation to HFNC (n = 50) versus conventional nasal cannula (n = 50) [65]. There were improved physiological variables of heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and SpO2/FiO2. In addition, fewer patients extubated to HFNC required reintubation (n = 2, 4% vs. n = 11, 22%). In the multicenter pilot RCT, FIRST-ABC, critically ill children were randomized to receive HFNC or CPAP [66]. One arm of the study evaluated the two modalities in recently extubated children. There were no differences in reintubation within 72 hours, PICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, or mortality. It is important to note that this was a pilot study and was, thus, likely to be underpowered to detect significant differences. Nonetheless, this manuscript does provide evi­ dence for further study in larger randomized trials that are currently ongoing [66].

The efficacy of HFNC in post-extubation respiratory failure has not been equivocally demonstrated in these small trials. Extubation to HFNC seems to improve some physiological variables in children. What these studies are lacking are vari­ ables that identify patients who are at risk of failure postextubation. The initial indications for intubation, duration of mechanical ventilation, level of sedation, and vital signs may predict failure or success of extubation to HFNC. Studies are needed to identify these markers and then design RCTs with a better-defined population. In addition, there are likely addi­ tional costs accrued if clinicians broadly treat patients with HFNC when it is likely that many patients may not need it.
3.6. Pediatric transport

Children with respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure present a unique challenge in transporting from one facility to another. The principles of basic resuscitation neces­ sitate the maintenance of an adequate airway. At times, elec­ tive endotracheal intubation is preferred given the risk of respiratory compromise during transport. Given the potential complications of intubation and invasive ventilation, other modalities such as noninvasive ventilation and HFNC are being evaluated as alternative treatment systems during interhospital transport. Transporting a patient with HFNC can be complicated. The heater and humidifier require a source of power and stable platform to ensure the system remains upright. In addition, it is conceivable, especially in larger patients requiring higher flows of gas, that ambulances may not have an adequate supply of oxygen or compressed air. Schlapbach and colleagues reviewed 793 infant transport cases and found a reduction in intubation and noninvasive ventilation corresponding to the added use of HFNC [67]. Importantly, the intubation rate during the first 24 hours of PICU admission did not change after the implementation and use of HFNC in the transport process.

Intra-hospital transport of critically ill children is associated with adverse events including, hypoxemia, bradycardia, tachy­ cardia, respiratory distress, hypotension, and cardiopulmonary arrest [68,69]. Children in the PICU are frequently transferred to and from the operating room, imaging suites, from the emergency department or general pediatric wards. Efforts to mitigate adverse events are important. Currently, there are no pediatric studies evaluating the use of HFNC in intra-hospital transport of critically ill children.

4. Conclusion

The use of HFNC has gained wide acceptance in PICUs in the treatment of children with acute respiratory illness. This is largely due to the perceived comfort to the patient and ease of use. In addition, many observational studies have demon­ strated benefits in physiological variables, including heart rate, respiratory rate, and SpO2. Other clinical outcomes, such as ICU and hospital length of stay, intubation rate, and mortality have shown modest improvements with HFNC or no differ­ ences when compared to standard oxygen therapy or nonin­ vasive ventilation. Given the heterogeneity of pediatric respiratory illnesses, larger prospective studies examining homogeneous populations are needed to prove clinical bene­ fit beyond vital sign improvement.
5. Expert opinion

The rapid adoption of HFNC for pediatric patients has largely been driven by small observational studies that have been generally consistent in showing a therapeutic benefit with respect to vital signs and clinical measures of the patient's work of breathing. However, with respect to patient-centered outcomes, such as intubation rates, mortality, or hospital length of stay, many studies were underpowered to detect a difference or show, at best, only modest improvements in clinical outcome. In addition, the perception that patient com­ fort is better with HFNC may cause providers to readily adopt this modality despite the lack of robust prospective clinical trials.

There is wide variability in practice with respect to flow settings and disease indications [70]. There are also a lack of studies evaluating indications for initiating, escalating, and weaning of HFNC therapy. While clinical guidelines have been associated with improved outcomes in the emergency department [44], no such studies exist in the PICU setting. The expansion of the use of HFNC on general wards and emergency departments, while apparently safe, may para­ doxically increase unnecessary usage [71,72], be more costly, and increase the risk of rare but catastrophic events [73], although additional investigations are needed. Without clear guidelines and protocols, it is conceivable that some chil­ dren are being over-treated in the hospital and length of stays (PICU and hospital) may be unnecessarily prolonged as we do not clearly understand the pertinent markers of improvement. Conversely, it is plausible that we are undertreating some children by using HFNC and potentially dan­ gerously delaying more definitive treatment. In addition, the use of HFNC on sick children on the general pediatric wards may delay timely transfer to the PICU, which may be asso­ ciated with adverse outcomes. Vital sign markers, heart rate and respiratory rate, have been identified as potential iden­ tifiers of HFNC responders [74]. Additional physiological or biochemical markers of response will be helpful to focus HFNC use in the optimal patients as well as avoid delays of more definitive treatment in HFNC non-responders.

Ideally, large multicenter randomized controlled trials examining HFNC in a variety of pediatric diseases are needed to conclusively prove the benefit(s) of HFNC. However, given the wide acceptance that already exists, designing such trials may be difficult because of the perceived lack of equipoise. Furthermore, deciding the appropriate comparator group is also difficult as the perception has been that HFNC is better than conventional oxygen and worse or equivalent to nonin­ vasive ventilation. Given the relatively low mortality of pedia­ tric respiratory diseases, studying such outcomes would require a very large number of patients across multiple sites, making recruitment of subjects likely impractical.

Despite these difficulties, it is important to continue research in this burgeoning field. Interpretation of earlier stu­ dies was often hampered by varying definitions of high flow and variable use of flow settings. Recent work has established that flows of 1-2 L/kg/min may be sufficient to treat many cases of acute bronchiolitis [20,42]. It is not yet understood if these same flow ranges are effective for pediatric pneumonia or asthma. With respect to asthma, in vitro studies have demonstrated variable nebulized drug deposition. Further research is needed in this area to optimize drug delivery.

The definition of PARDS requires the presence of CPAP greater than or equal to 5 cm H2O, thus precluding trials including HFNC. However, patients who are at risk of PARDS (i.e. meeting all the criteria except for the requirement of positive pressure) are a particularly interesting population that requires study. Traditionally, the optimal treatment is invasive mechanical ventilation with high PEEP and low tidal volume. Recent work in adults suggests that HFNC may be a modality that prevents patients at risk for ARDS from need­ ing intubation and may also reduce mortality [58]. Trials are needed in children who are at risk from PARDS to identify the safety and utility of HFNC in this group. Inevitably, some children would fail HFNC therapy and require invasive ventila­ tion. Studies identifying risk factors for failure are critically important.

Another avenue of research is through quality improve­ ment initiatives. If large multicenter studies are not feasible, then single-center quality improvement projects may be able to augment the growing literature. Charvat and colleagues enacted a multidisciplinary quality initiative over 3 years in infants with bronchiolitis treated with HFNC [75]. Through the implementation of an evidence-based weaning protocol, they were able to decrease HFNC length of treatment by 17 hours and hospital length of stay by 23 hours. During this period, there were no increases in PICU transfers or readmission rates after discharge.

While patient comfort and ease of use are important rea­ sons to choose a particular treatment modality, it may not promote optimal patient outcomes if those are the only rea­ sons. Currently, robust evidence of the efficacy of HFNC in treating the variety of pediatric critical illness is lacking. Some gains have been made, but much work remains to be done.

Background: Bronchiolitis is the most common reason for hospital admission in infants, with one third requiring oxygen therapy due to hypoxemia. It is unknown what proportion of hypoxemic infants with bronchiolitis can be managed with nasal high-flow in room air and their resulting outcomes.

Objectives and Settings: To assess the effect of nasal high-flow in room air in a subgroup of infants with bronchiolitis allocated to high-flow therapy in a recent multicenter randomized controlled trial.

Patients and Interventions: Infants allocated to the high-flow arm of the trial were initially treated with room air high-flow if saturations were ≥ 85%. Subsequently, if oxygen saturations did not increase to ≥ 92%, oxygen was added and FiO2 was titrated to increase the oxygen saturations. In this planned sub-study, infants treated during their entire hospital stay with high-flow room air only were compared to infants receiving either standard-oxygen or high-flow with oxygen. Baseline characteristics, hospital length of stay and length of oxygen therapy were compared.

Findings: In the per protocol analysis 64 (10%) of 630 infants commenced on highflow room air remained in room air only during the entire stay in hospital. These infants on high-flow room air were on average older and presented with moderate hypoxemia at presentation to hospital. Their length of respiratory support and length of stay was also significantly shorter. No pre-enrolment factors could be identified in a multivariable analysis.

INTRODUCTION

The application of oxygen for hypoxemia represents one of the most common medical and nursing interventions globally (1). Traditionally, oxygen was considered a safe intervention, but an increasing body of evidence demonstrates potential for harm in acute care settings including perinatal adaptation (2, 3), cardiac arrest (4), and acute stroke (5). Adverse effects of oxygen may relate to toxicity of free oxygen radicals, and adaptive mechanisms in health and disease (6-8). As a result, the application of oxygen as a drug is undergoing more scrutiny. Furthermore, access to oxygen in remote facilities and in low income countries can be problematic (9, 10).

The oxygen requirement in acute respiratory diseases leading to hypoxemia depends on several pathophysiological factors such as ventilation inhomogeneity, atelectasis, or consolidated lung parenchyma, an increased intra pulmonary shunt fraction and decreased alveolar-capillary membrane diffusion capacity (11). Traditionally, the first approach to improve hypoxemia consisted in increasing inspired oxygen fraction to treat the symptom whilst simultaneously searching for the cause of the hypoxemia. If this approach is ineffective then non-invasive, mainly continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or invasive ventilation strategies are commonly used in an incremental fashion, though both are highly resource and skill dependent (12). In contrast to oxygen alone, alveolar recruitment by provision of CPAP is likely to reverse or improve many conditions that lead to hypoxemia in children, whereas restricted oxygen diffusion due to thickened alveolar-capillary membrane is less commonly a feature early in the disease process. The application of CPAP however can be challenging, requires highly trained nursing and medical staff, is not always tolerated by patients, and therefore has been in the past restricted to intensive care unit (ICU) settings.

Nasal high-flow therapy, as a new positive airway pressure modality has been rapidly adopted in ICU, and subsequently in emergency departments (EDs) and general wards because of its ease of use (13-15). Physiological and clinical studies demonstrate a CPAP effect at high-flow rates that exceed peak inspiratory flow (16-18).

We recently published the findings of the Pediatric Acute Respiratory Intervention (PARIS) randomized controlled trial (RCT), which randomized 1,472 hypoxemic infants with bronchiolitis to either nasal high-flow therapy or standardoxygen therapy with the option to use rescue high-flow if infants failed standard-oxygen therapy (19). Nested within this RCT we addressed the pre-planned question whether high-flow therapy can normalize oxygenation without any increase in the FiO2 provided (20). METHODS

The protocol, methods, and results of the RCT have been described previously (19, 20). Briefly, 1,472 infants, < 12 months of age, admitted to 17 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand with bronchiolitis and an oxygen requirement were randomized in an open-label study design to treatment with standard subnasal oxygen or nasal high-flow (20). The primary outcome for the trial was treatment failure, defined by the presence of ≥ 3 of a possible 4 abnormal physiological parameters, and escalation of care. The trial confirmed that treatment failure and escalation of care occurred in fewer patients randomized to highflow compared with standard-oxygen ( p < 0.001). The trial was undertaken between October 2013 and August 2016, and the relevant human research ethics committee at each participating site approved the study (HREC/13/QRCH/93). Informed written consent was obtained by parent or guardian.

The primary objective of this pre-specified sub-study was to test if the oxygen requirement can be reversed in infants with bronchiolitis, by the provision of room air high-flow alone. For this purpose, the study protocol required that all infants, who were allocated to the high-flow arm, and with enrolment oxygen saturation between 85 and ≤ 92/94%, to be initially commenced on high-flow room air (FiO2 0.21) at 2 L/kg/min via ageappropriate Optiflow Junior TM cannula and Airvo2 TM high-flow system (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare; Auckland, New Zealand). If high-flow room air had failed to achieve target saturations of ≥ 92% in participating tertiary children's hospitals, and ≥ 94% in secondary hospitals (saturation targets were set by individual institution's standard current practice and not specified centrally by the trial investigators) after 10 min the FiO2 of the highflow system was increased to achieve the target saturation. Highflow room air was stopped (i.e., flow rate reduced from 2 to 0 L/kg/min without gradual reduction) as soon as clinicians saw clinical improvement and participant's oxygen saturation was maintained at ≥ 92/94% for at least 4 h. For those infants receiving nasal high-flow oxygen, the FiO2 was titrated to keep saturations between a 92/94 and 98% target, and once on highflow room air for 4 h and maintaining target saturations, highflow therapy was stopped. If infants subsequently developed a further oxygen requirement, according to their institution's definition, high-flow was instigated using the same procedures as at initiation of high-flow at randomization. Infants allocated to standard-oxygen therapy received 100% subnasal oxygen up to a maximum of 2 L/min to maintain oxygen saturations within the same targets as the high-flow arm. All other bronchiolitis specific therapies were at the discretion of the treating clinician.

Oxygen Therapy Groups (Figure 1)

We defined four oxygen therapy groups for this sub-study. Infants allocated to standard-oxygen remained on subnasal standard-oxygen (standard-oxygen group) unless they required escalation of care, which in most of these infants was achieved by using high-flow with oxygen. Infants allocated to high-flow with saturations < 85% at randomization received immediate highflow with oxygen (high-flow with immediate oxygen group). The threshold of 85% was chosen in consensus with the participating hospitals. Infants allocated to high-flow presenting with saturations between 85 and ≤ 92/94% were started on highflow room air. Infants without improved oxygenation (saturation ≤ 92/94%) after 10 min on high-flow room air were switched to high-flow with oxygen (high-flow with oxygen group) whereas infants who improved their saturations to ≥ 92/94% remained on high-flow room air (high-flow room air group).
Study Outcomes

The primary outcomes were: first a proof of concept to demonstrate whether a subgroup of hypoxemic infants with bronchiolitis can be treated with high-flow room air only while maintaining their target saturations; and secondly to determine the proportion of hypoxemic infants with bronchiolitis that respond to high-flow in room air. Secondary outcomes included differences in basic demographics, risk factors such as prematurity and pre-existing disease, virus detected, severity of disease at randomization, length of hospital stay, and length of high-flow therapy. The physiological response of heart and respiratory rate to high-flow room air was analyzed for the first 3 days of admission. In one of the participating hospitals all data on the change of respiratory and heart rate, and saturation of all infants enrolled were also obtained relating to the first hour of oxygen therapy post start of the intervention ( Table 2 ).

The sub-group of infants receiving high-flow room air only were compared to the three oxygen groups; infants on standard oxygen, infants on high-flow with immediate oxygen, and infants high-flow with oxygen.

RESULTS

In the original RCT, 1,472 infants with bronchiolitis were randomized and subsequently provided written consent; in the per protocol analysis 710 received standard-oxygen and 746 received high-flow of which 52 (7%) commenced on high-flow with immediate oxygen, 630 (70%) commenced high-flow room air with a later increase of FiO2 and 64 (9%) received high-flow room air ( Figure 1 ). Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of the infants in high-flow room air compared to infants on highflow with immediate oxygen, high-flow with oxygen and infants treated with standard-oxygen therapy. There were a number of statistical differences in several of the pre-enrolment factors between the three study groups ( Table 1 ): the distribution of age at enrolment was significantly different between the treatment groups with the proportion of infants < 3 months of age lowest in the high-flow room air (17.2%), the body weight was highest in the high-flow room air group, followed by the standardoxygen group and then high-flow in oxygen. Infants on highflow with immediate oxygen received more frequently antibiotics and sedation. Infants in the high-flow room air group showed higher oxygen saturation pre-enrolment than infants in the other groups ( Table 2 ). In the cohort of infants ( n = 334) in which physiological parameters were measured within the first hour of treatment, infants on standard-oxygen showed the highest saturations. The changes in saturation, heart and respiratory rate in infants on high-flow room air are shown for the first 72 h in Figures 2 , 3 .

The length of hospital stay was shortest in infants in the highflow room air group ( Table 2 ). None of the tested pre-enrolment factors such as age, prematurity, RSV , time of onset of disease to presentation or heart nor respiratory rate were predictive for a success of high-flow room air therapy ( Table 3 ).

None of the infants on high-flow room air required intensive care admission and no adverse events were observed in either the high-flow room air group or those who commenced treatment initially in room air.

For completeness, infants in the standard-oxygen group presenting with pre-enrolment saturations < 85%were compared to infants with saturations between 85 and ≤ 92/94% and the comparison is shown in Table 4 . Similarly, to the high-flow group, infants in the standard-oxygen arm presenting with pre-enrolment saturations of < 85% were younger and had lower body weight. The infants in the standard-oxygen group and presenting with saturations < 85% received similarly to the patients in the high-flow with immediate oxygen group, significantly more antibiotics and sedation.
DISCUSSION

The World Health Organization recommended in 2012 that effective oxygen delivery systems should be a universal standard of care and should be made more widely available (21). At the same time, an increasing body of evidence suggests potential for harm related to oxygen application in various settings including perinatal adaptation, cardiac arrest, and intensive care (2-5). Furthermore, in adults receiving mechanical ventilation it has been shown that a large number of patients were left on unnecessarily high inspired oxygen fraction, which can contribute to lung disease (22). Bronchiolitis represents the most common disease leading to non-elective admission of infants and oxygen remains the mainstay of therapy for this patient group (23). Our data demonstrates that in a small subgroup of hypoxemic infants with bronchiolitis the oxygen requirement can be safely treated with high-flow in room air for their entire hospital stay. Infants responding to high-flow room air not only showed a significant improvement in their saturations but also a reduction in heart and respiratory rates indicating effective respiratory support ( Figures 2 , 3 ). The reversal of the hypoxemia was likely due to the positive airway pressure effect generated by nasal high-flow therapy, which improved the underlying pathophysiology such as ventilation maldistribution and loss of lung volume (atelectasis). Previous physiological studies have shown that high-flow rates at 2 L/kg/min generate a positive airway pressure in the range of 4-6 cm H2O, which can restore the patient's functional residual capacity and reduce ventilation inhomogeneity (24, 25).

The current recommendations for first line treatment of hypoxemia is the provision of oxygen (26). If supplemental oxygen is ineffective, then as a second line treatment some form of positive pressure ventilation either non-invasive or invasive ventilation should be used. The study design and outcomes in the high-flow arm suggests it is safe to initially institute high-flow in room air and to subsequently supplement oxygen in those who need it, except in infants with severe hypoxemia on presentation (saturation < 85%). The results of this prospective trial indicate that a small proportion of infants (10%) will respond to high-flow room air alone, and those requiring oxygen can be safely titrated to the appropriate dose. Albeit a small proportion of infants in our study cohort responded to high-flow room air, these findings provide as a first interesting physiological proof of concept that in these infants oxygenation can be improved by providing positive airway pressure only.

A multivariate analysis did not demonstrate any predictive factors for responders of this approach. Infants who required high-flow room air only had a significantly shorter stay in hospital, most likely as a result of a milder form of the respiratory disease.

The results of our study serve as a proof of concept that may inform future clinical trials particularly in less well-resourced settings where access to oxygen is limited. This could prove beneficial for regions where the mortality of infants with chest infections and an oxygen requirement is 8% (African FEAST trial) (27, 28). A recent study in Bangladesh compared standard-oxygen, bubble CPAP, and high-flow in children with chest infections aged up to 5 years. The median saturation at presentation in this study was 86 % (IQR 82-88) with only 14% of enrolled children having a saturation of < 85% (29). The current COAST trial being performed in Uganda and Kenya in children presenting with a chest infection and an oxygen requirement is currently investigating if high-flow in room air can reverse hypoxemia and reduce mortality (28).

One of the shifts in paradigm in this study was that oxygen therapy was started from 'low'-in room air-and titrated up to reach the desired SpO2 threshold > 92/94% whereas traditionally oxygen therapy was introduced from 'high' to achieve maximal saturations and then titrated down. It is likely that the titrate up strategy will mean that saturation levels will be maintained closer to the lower acceptable levels than in the titrate down strategy. Hyperoxia is commonly observed in mechanically ventilated patients and most often related to the reluctance of clinicians to reduce the inspired oxygen fraction (22). In the small cohort of infants in whom physiological parameters were also measured within the first hour of treatment, the oxygen saturations were highest in the standard-oxygen group. In the high-flow group the clinicians were instructed to start with low FiO2 (room air) and only increase if required, whereas in the standard-oxygen group no instructions were given.
Limitations

The medical records in the participating sites did not allow measuring the fidelity if clinicians strictly adhered to the proposed high-flow room air approach, hence the proportion of patients who would have benefitted from the high-flow room air approach may have been greater. Our study protocol used a saturation target between 92 and 98% (in some centers 94-98%). WHO is recommending a lower threshold of 90% to initiate oxygen therapy. Therefore, using a lower treatment threshold for hypoxemia would have likely increased the proportion of successful treatments with high-flow in room air. A recent study in bronchiolitis in the UK showed that keeping a threshold of 90% compared to 94% did not impact on safety and efficacy (30).
CONCLUSION

A small proportion of infants with bronchiolitis and hypoxemia who were admitted to hospital did respond to nasal high-flow therapy using room air only. The clinical improvement of the high-flow therapy could be demonstrated immediately with decreased heart and respiratory rate. Nasal highflow room air therapy may be a valuable option to treat hypoxemia in bronchiolitis in settings with limited access to oxygen.

EVIDENCE BEFORE THIS STUDY

A comprehensive literature search using MEDLINE, Cochrane, CINAHL,andEMBASEdemonstrated that high-flow therapy has clinical benefit over standard oxygen therapy used in infants with bronchiolitis in general ward settings with two large randomized controlled trials showing a reduced need to escalate therapy. No study could be identified to investigate the role of high-flow in room air and its clinical effect.

IMPLICATIONS OF ALL THE AVAILABLE EVIDENCE

This study presents as a first a novel concept to improve hypoxemia in infants with bronchiolitis. The approach is to first apply positive airway pressure support followed by increasing the oxygen fraction if required. Titration of oxygen from low to normal saturation as a mean to limit possible oxygen toxicity.

Address for correspondence Steve Cunningham, MBChB, PhD, FRCP, FRCPCH, Department of Paediatric Respiratory Medicine, MRC Centre for Inflammation Research, Queen ' s Medical Research Institute, University of Edinburgh, 47 Little France Crescent, Edinburgh EH16 4TJ, United Kingdom (e-mail: steve.cunningham@ed.ac.uk).

Acute viral lower respiratory tract infection is frequently associated with hypoxemia and respiratory distress, sometimes progressing to hypercarbia and respiratory failure. In recent years, trials have assessed the effects of oxygen supplementation and respiratory support with high-flow oxygen therapy. An oxygen saturation target of 90% is as safe and clinically effective as 94% in infants with bronchiolitis. Trials of highflow humidified oxygen have demonstrated safety, but as yet poorly demarcated an appropriate place for use within the clinical course of the disease. Effective trials of continuous positive airway pressure are lacking and urgently required. The trials reported to date have highlighted the need for common outcomes in relation to treatment failure.

Viral lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in infants is the mostcommonconditionassociatedwithadmissiontohospital in the first year of life. In the 80 years since its principal description, 1 bronchiolitis has changed little, with the exception of fewer deaths for children with the condition in developedhealthcarecomparedwithdevelopinghealthcare. 2 With no effective treatments, the key change over time has been improvements in supportive care, hydration, and respiratory support. As viral upper respiratory tract infection progresses toanLRTI,tachypnea,hypoxemia,hypercarbia,andrespiratory failure may require support to tide over the period of illness until recovery occurs. Hydration aside, which can be nasogastric or intravenous, both of which appearequallyeffective, 3 it is the widespread availability of supplemental oxygen, positive airway pressure, and intensive care support that has contributed most to improved outcomes over time.
Oxygen Saturation Targets and Outcome in Lower Respiratory Tract Infection

Supplemental oxygen for respiratory disease became widespread in western health care in the 1950s and was provided liberally with little ability to monitor. Supplemental oxygen has a clear benefit in improving outcomes in acute LRTI, 4 but less clear is how much supplemental oxygen is required to support children with LRTI. 5 In obstructive sleep apnea, chronic recurrent hypoxemia has been associated with cognitive deficits, 6 and infants with chronic lung disease of prematurity have higher mortality when target oxygen saturation margins differ by just 3%. 7 Hypoxemia is common in children with bronchiolitis. Arriving at the emergency department (ED), 40% of infants have an SpO2 below 94% and 10 to 16% have SpO2 below 90%. 8,9 During hospital admission, 73% of infants are provided with supplemental oxygen at a 94% SpO2 threshold and 56% of infants when a 90% target is applied. 9 The Bronchiolitis of Infancy Discharge Study (BIDS) compared a recommended normal oxygen saturation in health 10 ( > 94%) versus the World Health Organization recommended SpO2 ( > 90%), which was also adopted by the United States Academy of Pediatrics in their Bronchiolitis guideline of 2005. 11 The BIDS trial of 615 infants with bronchiolitis identified equivalence of time to symptom resolution (no cough, which is the principal symptom in bronchiolitis) in a double-blind randomized controlled trial. 9 Unexpectedly, other clinical outcomes were better in infants managed with a lower oxygen saturation target, including the time to return to adequate feeding, time back to normal, and fewer infants requiring readmission to hospital and antibiotics postdischarge. These positive outcomes led sometosuggest that supplemental oxygen may have adverse

effects on viral replication or host defenses. Further oxygen saturation target studies could be ethically challenging below 90% saturation in developed health care. A study currently in progress may provide some insight: the Children ' s Oxygen Administration Strategies Trial (COAST) study is assessing SpO2 targets as low as 80% in health care settings where resources are severely limited. 12
Supportive Management of Respiratory Distress

Respiratory distress is common, essentially pathognomic, in LRTI and bronchiolitis. Inflammation and mucous plugging of the bronchioles, combined with a compliant chest wall, creates additional work of breathing and retractions. Many infants, particularly over 6 months of age, often have the capacity to tolerate long periods of dyspnea before spontaneous improvement sets in. Supplemental oxygen does not relieve respiratory distress. 13

Historically, limitedcriticalcare capacityrationedthe use of (nasal) continuouspositive airway pressure (CPAP) support for infants with LRTI and respiratory distress. With options limited, infants who recovered either with low-flow supplemental oxygen or with increasing respiratory failure were trialed onCPAPtostave off intubation and ventilation. 14 Caring for an infant with respiratory distress is distressing for parents and staff, and the wish to alleviate any dyspnea is understandable. High-flow humidified oxygen (HFOT, variably termed) blends highly humidified oxygen and air at higher flow rates than traditional low-flow oxygen. The result is considered to provide greater comfort in breathing and to enable a higher inspired oxygen (typically up to 60% FiO2) when compared with low-flow oxygen (typically 30 -38% FiO2). The flow does provide some degree of positive airway pressure, but this is mostlikely in the order of 2 to 3 cm H20 and not 6 to 10 cm H2O that CPAP units would generate in the airway. HFOT is thereforeoftenprovidedtogiveperceivedbenefittopatientcomfort and to reduce work of breathing.
Supporting Respiratory Failure with Hypercarbia

With LRTI progression, tiring respiratory muscles lead to respiratory failure, heralded by hypercarbia (defined generally as pCO2 > 6.5kPa/50 mm Hg). Applying positive airway pressure can open blocked and inflamed airways, enhancing ventilation and airway clearance. CPAP can be applied by nasal maskor prongs and has been available for more than 20 years. Disappointingly, there are no effective studies of CPAP use in bronchiolitis in a developed health care setting. Observational studies suggest benefits in improving ventilation (reducing hypercarbia 14 and respiratory rate 15 ). Once again, colleagues working in developing health care may provide evidence to structure our approach, with one trial completed and one in progress to assess bubble CPAP in respiratory failure. 16,17 TherearenotrialsofmechanicalventilationinLRTIinchildren. Atrial is in progress to assess the effect of exogenoussurfactant in children ventilated with acute bronchiolitis.
Thresholds for Intervening in Bronchiolitis Are Changing

When care options were limited to low-flow oxygen or critical care CPAP, clinical thresholds were mostly objective. Hypoxemia as a driver for low flow supplemental oxygen, objectively measured by pulse oxygen saturation monitoring. A trial of CPAP to support respiratory failure, objectively measured by blood gas carbon dioxide. Variance in practice appears increasingly determined by subjective clinical interpretation of respiratory distress, which is difficult to standardize (by clinical scoring or other means).

Admissions to critical care have increased considerably over recent years (together with associated costs), despite stable mortality rates and no understood change in respiratory syncytial virus pathogenicity. 18 Rate of admission and practice is highly variable between countries (4 -18%) and between critical care units. 19,20 While some increase in critical care use relates to additional intervention in children with complex health care needs, most variability in critical care appears to be related to differing clinical thresholds for intervention. The arrival of HFOT appears to have added to this variance, as the introduction to clinical care has been more rapid than the ability to assess its merits.

HFOT is being widely introduced to the clinical space between hypoxemia controlled by low-flow oxygen and hypercarbic respiratory failure. The ability of HFOT to enhance oxygenation and improve ventilation has been demonstrated in animal models. 21 The question is not quite whether it can do these things, but what population requires to be served by something additional to lowflow oxygen through a nasal cannula (2l/minute) or CPAP. This is a health and economic consideration as HFOT may be provided in ward-based settings, whereas CPAP is most commonly provided in critical care settings. HFOT established itself in neonatal care 22 and has rapidly extended to infants with acute LRTI. Observational studies suggest that HFOT may reduce work of breathing, but that is not objectively demonstrated, and the effect of reducing work of breathing on other health outcomes (time in oxygen, time to discharge, time to resolution of symptoms) is unproven. 23
Randomized Trials of High-Flow Humidified Oxygen and Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
Thefirst randomized controlled trials of HFOT in infants with acute LRTI have recently been reported.

An open-label study assigned 202 children in hospital pediatric wards with moderate bronchiolitis to either lowflow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen (maximum 2l/minute c30 -38% FiO2) or HFOT (maximum 11/kg/minute c60% FiO2). The study identified that HFOT did not result in faster weaning from supplemental oxygen nor a faster time to discharge. 24 A significantly higher number of children had a failure of treatment in the low-flow oxygen group when compared with those in the HFOT group. However, the number requiring critical care support was equivalent. The trial demonstrates that early use of HFOT does not alter the clinical course of acute bronchiolitis.

The Tramontane study randomly assigned 142 children in a pediatric intensive care setting with moderate/severe acute viral bronchiolitis to either open-label nasal CPAP (7 cmH2O) or HFOT (2l/kg/minute). 25 This noninferiority trial demonstrated that HFOT was noninferior to nasal CPAP in terms of treatment failure: 31% failed in the nasal CPAP group (22 of 71 infants) compared with 51% (36 of 71 infants) in the HFNC group, which did not meet the prespecified limits for noninferiority. A posthoc superiority analysis suggested that CPAP was superior to HFOT. A study within an ED randomly assigned 60 children to helmet CPAP ( n ¼ 20) compared with HFOT ( n ¼ 20) or control ( n ¼ 20, presumed low-flow oxygen). 26 A large proportion of the included infants were diagnosed with bronchiolitis (77%), with the remainder with pneumonia and asthma. Children were included if they had respiratory distress on arrival at ED. CPAP had faster improvement in pH and pCO2 with a shorter duration of hospitalization, whereas HFOT had faster improvements in FiO2. Groups were not well balanced at baseline for age or weight, with HFOT allocated to older and heavier children. In a developing tertiary hospital health care setting, a trial randomly assigned 225 children under 5 years of age with pneumonia and hypoxemia to either bubble CPAP ( N ¼ 79; 35%), HFOT ( N ¼ 67; 30%), or low-flow oxygen therapy ( N ¼ 79; 35%). 16 The trial was stopped prematurely by a data monitoring committee as fewer deaths occurred in the CPAP group ( N ¼ 3, 4%) compared with the HFOT ( N ¼ 10, 13%) or low-flow oxygen therapy ( N ¼ 10, 15%) group. At the time of closure of the study, there were treatment failures in 6% ( N ¼ 5) of CPAP, 13% ( N ¼ 10) of HFOT, and 14% ( N ¼ 16) of low-flow oxygen therapy participants.

The PARIS (Paediatric Acute Respiratory Intervention Study) trial is the largest trial to date of HFOT in moderate/ acute bronchiolitis. 27 In total, 1,400 hospitalized infants have been randomized to receive either HFOT or low-flow oxygen therapy. The primary outcome is treatment failure. The study is anticipated to report within 2018. Striking about all these studies is that treatment failure is variably defined, and success or failure is predicated on nonstandardized definitions of treatment failure.
What Is Treatment Failure in Acute Lower Respiratory Tract Infection?

There are no common agreed definitions of what would constitute a failure of treatment in acute LRTI, apart from death. Death is uncommon in term and healthy infants in developed health care 28 and could not be considered except in resource-poor settings.

The factors used to identify treatment failure for recent trials of respiratory support in LRTI are given in ► Table 1 . Unfortunately, outcomes used to date have had inadequate validation as clinical surrogate biomarkers, that is, the association between the treatment failure outcomes and clinical risk.

Future Directions

Further trials to standardize the delivery of respiratory support in bronchiolitis are required. These may include standardizing the delivery of respiratory support, including targets, weaning strategies, and stopping rules. A trial of CPAP in developed health care is urgently required, including assessments of use outside critical care areas. Thresholds for treatment failure should be defined, ensuring that they relate to risk, so that valuable resources are appropriately allocated and treatments are provided to those most in need.

High flow nasal cannula therapy in children: working principles and treatment failure predictors

1. Introduction

Historically, Standard Oxygen Therapy (SOT) is provided on low flow ≤ 2 L/min oxygen, without or with very little cold bubble humidification in the Emergency Department (ED) and in Pediatric Wards (PW), which is not capable of delivering the optimum hydration level at the most favorable function of the respiratory system. The exact amount of oxygen administration is rarely known and approximations are made depending on the oxygen flow and the air mixing from the environment, according to the peak inspiratory flow generated by the patient's respiratory effort. A system that could deliver a warm, well-hydrated, precise oxygen level, would have been ideal.
Abstract

High Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) delivers high flowrates of a heated air/oxygen fresh gas breathing mixture, in an open system, at the exact amount of fraction inspired oxygen, and at the optimum hydration level. By definition, due to high flow rates, higher than 2 L/min, it produces a wash out of the anatomic dead space and the End-tidal Carbon dioxide (EtCO 2 ), and augments thus effective alveolar ventilation at the same rate of minute ventilation, helping reduce partial arterial pressure of Carbon dioxide (PaCO 2 ) levels. Although depending on mouth closure and the relative size of the nasal cannula prongs related to nares, it produces a minimum Positive End Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) level, which is especially helpful in keeping unstable alveoli open, recruiting lung volume, and increasing the functional residual capacity. It reduces respiratory resistance and the high work of breathing which is a common feature in patients with respiratory failure. But its most important characteristics are the ease of implementation and good patient tolerance. It has emerged as a promising support mode in the last decade, and its use is being continuously expanded. Although it started from neonates, it expanded to children and adults, and tested in all causes of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, especially in bronchiolitis, and in post-extubation respiratory failure as well, starting from Emergency Department (ED), Pediatric Ward (PW), Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU), and during transportation. Comparisons and meta-analyses, although not of equal modalities, have shown that it is definitely better than Standard Oxygen Therapy (SOT), and rather inferior to Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). The aim of the present study is to explore the HFNC position in the timeline of recommendations for mechanical ventilation in critically ill children. We present a review on HFNC literature evidence in patients aged 1 month to 18 years, focusing on its mechanism of action, clinical effects, and timely recognition of treatment failure predictors.
Keywords
High flow nasal cannula-HFNC; Working principles; Treatment failure predictors; Pediatric intensive care unit-PICU; Infants; Children

In children, severe pulmonary ( e.g. , pneumonia), or extra pulmonary ( e.g. , sepsis) illnesses, would lead to acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) and Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (PARDS) [1, 2], where an initial amount of Positive End Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) is desirable in halting the progression of the disease. A system that could deliver easily, by hand, a minimum initial level of PEEP at the onset of critical illness, would have been highly desirable.

Invasive Mechanical Ventilation (IMV) [3, 4], the key treatment in the majority of Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) patients, is inevitably linked to the undesired effects of the sedation and the increased risk of developing Ventilator Associated Events (VAE) [5, 6]. Thus, an alternative is sought in the form of non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV) [7, 8], under proper monitoring for a timely recognition of NIV failure, as delay in intubation is also linked to worse outcome. In mechanically ventilated patients the most challenging period is around weaning and extubation [9]. Even under the most favorable conditions, Post Extubation Respiratory Failure (PERF) [10] happens in about 10-20% of cases and in many of them NIV could be used as a rescue therapy as well, to avoid reintubation. NIV could be delivered by Intensive Care Unit (ICU) ventilators (as Non Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation-NIPPV) and/or special devices that could deliver Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) and/or Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure (BIPAP) ventilation. Although not identical, High Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) therapy, with its distinct properties, could be considered as a preliminary form of NIV, which could also help to overcome some situations of respiratory failure, either as a first line treatment or as a rescue therapy for PERF.
